title: Preface
text:
How this book works
This book is for public health practitioners who already know how to do the work — the epidemiology, the surveillance, the briefings — but are being asked to do it in R. Maybe your agency is moving off SAS. Maybe a collaborator handed you a .R file and you want to understand it. Maybe you’ve opened RStudio, stared at a blank script, and closed it again.
This book is not a general introduction to R. It is not a statistics textbook. It will not teach you epidemiology. It assumes you already have domain knowledge and gives you the R fluency to apply it.
This book has one job: get a practicing epidemiologist writing, running, and sharing R-based analyses as fast as possible.
Every chapter builds on one analysis: a COVID-19 briefing for a state health commissioner. You start with a raw CSV and a blank folder. By the end, you have a self-updating report that pulls live data and publishes itself. Each chapter introduces exactly one new skill and shows you why it earns its place in the workflow — not as an exercise, but as a real improvement to something you built yourself in the chapter before.
Work through the chapters in order. They are designed to be read with R open in front of you, running the code as you go.

title: 1  Modern R and Public Health
text:
1.1 Why R
Public health work is converging on R. This chapter gets your workspace ready so chapter 1 can start with code.
If your agency runs SAS, you already know the core loop: read data in, reshape it, summarize it, output it. R does the same thing. The difference is everything around that loop.
Free. No license. No seat-count negotiation with procurement. No renewal cycle. R runs on a laptop, a server, or a cloud VM — same tool, same code.
Analysis lives in a script. Every step is recorded. Six months later you run the same file and get the same answer. When the Commissioner asks “where did this number come from,” you show the code.
Reports update themselves. Quarto — the tool this book is built with — embeds code directly in a document. Change a number upstream and the table in the PDF changes with it. No more copy-pasting from Excel into Word.
The public health ecosystem is here. CDC, state health departments, and academic epi groups publish R code. Reading it — and writing it — is a basic competency the field is converging on.
The tidyverse maps to what you already know. SAS DATA steps and PROC steps have direct equivalents:
Syntax changes. Mental model mostly doesn’t.

1.2 How this works
Every chapter builds on one analysis: a COVID-19 briefing for a Connecticut health commissioner. You start with a raw CSV and an empty folder. Chapter by chapter the analysis gains new capabilities — until at the end you have a self-updating report that anyone on your team could run.
Each chapter introduces exactly one new skill. The skill earns its place by solving a real problem in the analysis — not as an exercise, but as a genuine improvement to what you built before.
Code along. Every code block in this book is meant to be run, not just read. Open R before you start each chapter and keep it open.
One thing to know about R before you start: unlike SAS, R is interactive. When you run code, results appear immediately in your session. Objects — datasets, plots, numbers — live in memory and you can inspect them at any time. Think of it less like submitting a batch job and more like a conversation with your data.

title: 1  Modern R and Public Health
text:
1.7 The scenario
The pandemic is in full swing and you are working as an analyst for the Connecticut Department of Public Health’s Pandemic Incident Command. You are tasked with preparing a briefing for the Commissioner so that they can in turn brief the governor on the current situation.
The first standing question is this: Is it getting worse in Hartford, or not?
Today we are going to answer that question, click by click. Slowly we will build up our R knowledge and reduce friction until we have an analysis we can share with others.

1.7.1 Folder Structure
It is good practice to stick with a common folder layout for each of your projects. Different programming languages have different conventions but many layouts are very similar. This reduces the cognitive load for yourself and others when navigating larger projects. There are tools for creating, saving, and sharing project templates, but for now we will do this by hand.

Create a new folder called covid-briefing wherever you keep projects.
Inside it, create these folders one at a time:

data
R
scripts
outputs
docs

Inside data, create two more folders: raw and processed.
Inside outputs, create two more folders: figures and tables.

At the end you should have a folder structure that looks like this:
covid-briefing/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv   ← you'll add this shortly
│   └── processed/
├── R/
├── scripts/
├── outputs/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
└── docs/
Why these specific folders?








Folder
Purpose
Rule




data/raw
Exactly what you downloaded
Never edit a file in here.


data/processed
Cleaned data you can trust
Always regenerable from raw + a script


R
Reusable functions
Empty today — used once you stop copy-pasting


scripts
Numbered analysis steps
01_, 02_, … so the order is obvious


outputs/figures
Plots
Never hand-edited; always regenerated

Summary CSVs etc…
Same rule as figures


docs
Reports
Empty today — used when you build the briefing doc





1.7.2 Open the Project in Your IDE
Once the folders exist, open the project in RStudio or Positron so that every path you write in code is relative to covid-briefing/, not to your Desktop or Downloads folder.
RStudio: File → New Project → Existing Directory → select covid-briefing → Create Project.
Positron: File → Open Folder → select covid-briefing.
Either way, the IDE will reopen with covid-briefing as your working directory. This matters throughout the rest of the book.


1.7.3 Getting the Data

Go to the Open Data dataset page: Covid 19 Tests, Cases and Deaths by Town ARCHIVE
Click Export → CSV to download it.
Move the downloaded file into data/raw/.
Rename it to include the date you downloaded it, e.g.: ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv







Tip



Every dataset this book uses — with its source page and direct download links — is cataloged in the Data Library at the end of the book. If you ever need to find or re-download source data, that’s where to look.


The date stamp matters more than it looks like it should. This dataset is revised after the fact — Connecticut DPH updates prior dates as new reports come in. Stamping the filename is how you’ll later be able to say “this analysis used the data as it existed on this date,” which is exactly the kind of question a Commissioner will ask you.
From this point forward: never open this file and edit it by hand. If something about it needs to change, that change happens in a script, not in the file itself.






Note



Want to check your folder structure against a reference? See project-snapshots/after-ch-00 on GitHub for what covid-briefing/ should look like at this point.

Workspace is ready, data is in data/raw/. Next chapter: write your first R code.

title: 2  Loading Your First Dataset
text:
2.1 Packages
Your workspace is set up and your raw data is sitting in data/raw/. Time to write your first R code.
R ships with a base set of tools. On top of that, the community has built thousands of packages — collections of ready-made code you can install and use without writing everything yourself. These are distributed through CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network), R’s official package repository.
The family of packages we’ll lean on most is called the tidyverse — a curated set of tools that share a common design and work well together. We’ll introduce them one at a time. This chapter uses two of them plus one helper for building file paths.

text:
2.2 Reading Data Files

2.2.1 Reading our Comma Delimited File (.csv)
We are going to do a few things here:

Load the packages we need into our session.
Build a path to our data file and save it as csv_path.
Read the data into our session and save it as covid_data.


library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(here)



2.2.2 Paths and here()
Before reading the file, a word on paths — because this is where R trips people up early.
When you run code interactively, R looks for files starting from your project root (wherever your .Rproj file lives or the root of the folder you opened your with your IDE). You’ll often need to reference files that live somewhere other than the project root. Hardcoding a full path like /home/my-username/folder-that-only-i-have/r-file.R ties your project to one specific computer. That’s not ideal, which is why building paths relative to the project root matters.
here() from the here package fixes both problems. It detects your project root and always builds paths from there, regardless of how or where the code runs. Reach for it any time you’re building a path to a data file, instead of pasting in a full path from your own machine or typing a relative path like "data/raw/file.csv" that quietly breaks the moment your working directory isn’t where you assumed it was.

# here() takes folder names as separate arguments.
# It joins them with the correct separator for your OS.
csv_path <- here("data", "raw", "ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv")

covid_data <- read_csv(csv_path)

3.2 The pipe
Before diving in, one piece of syntax you’ll see throughout this book:

# The pipe |> passes the result of one step into the next.
# Read it as "and then."
covid_data |>
  filter(Town == "Hartford")

# is the same as:
filter(covid_data, Town == "Hartford")

Coming from SAS, think of it like chaining DATA steps and PROC steps without writing an intermediate dataset between each one.

3.7 Step 5 — Computing daily new cases
total_cases is a running total — it only ever goes up. To see whether things are getting worse day to day, we need the change between one report and the next, not the running total itself. lag() shifts a column down by one row, so total_cases - lag(total_cases) gives “today’s total minus yesterday’s total” — the daily new cases.

hartford <-
  hartford |>
  mutate(new_cases = total_cases - lag(total_cases))

tail(hartford, 14)

The very first row has no “yesterday” to subtract, so lag() gives it NA there — expected, not a bug.






WarningHandle “as reported” data with care



new_cases here is only as good as the reporting behind it. Real pandemic data was reported in batches — weekends and holidays often showed artificially low counts followed by a backlog dump on the next business day, and health departments regularly went back and revised earlier totals as duplicate tests were removed or late results came in. That means new_cases can come out negative on a day when a correction lowered a previous total, even though nothing was actually “un-reported.” This wasn’t a quirk of this dataset specifically — it was one of the most persistent, genuinely frustrating problems in tracking COVID-19 nationally. It’s worth remembering any time “new cases” is computed by subtracting two “as of” snapshots instead of coming from a system that recorded each case on the day it actually happened.

title: 4  Cleaning Data
text:
4.1 Installing Packages
Real data is rarely clean. Column names are inconsistent, values need reshaping, text fields need tidying up, and dates need parsing before they’re ready for analysis. This chapter covers four packages that handle the bulk of that work.
install.packages(c(
  "janitor", # for cleaning names and basic data cleaning
  "tidyr", # for reshaping data
  "stringr", # for working with text
  "glue", # for string interpolation
  "lubridate" # for working with dates
))
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(here)
library(janitor)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)
library(glue)
Data come in all shapes and sizes, and it is difficult to come up with a single approach that will fit every situation. However, there are some common patterns that show up frequently in public health data. This chapter will cover some of the most common data cleaning tasks and the R packages that can help you accomplish them.
# load up our raw data
csv_path <- here("data", "raw", "ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv")
covid_data <- read_csv(csv_path)

title: 4  Cleaning Data
text:
4.2 janitor
By now you’ve probably noticed that the column names in our covid_data aren’t very easy to work with. They contain spaces and mixed case that are difficult to reference due to R’s case-sensitive nature. Other data may have special characters, punctuation, or extra white space in the names of their columns.
The janitor package has a function called clean_names() that can help with this. It will convert column names to lower case, replace spaces with underscores, and remove special characters. This makes it much easier to work with the data in R. You could recreate this functionality from scratch, but clean_names() is a convenient and well-tested function that saves time and effort and is such an easy package to recommend.
Recall the names of our covid_data:

#subset of the names
names(covid_data) |> head(5)

[1] "Last update date" "Town number"      "Town"             "Total cases"     
[5] "Confirmed cases" 



covid_clean <-
  covid_data |>
  clean_names()

names(covid_clean) |> head(5)

[1] "last_update_date" "town_number"      "town"             "total_cases"     
[5] "confirmed_cases" 


A single function call - it is that simple. The janitor package has a lot of other useful functions for cleaning, and even presenting data in a more readable format. We’ll cover some of those later, but it’s worth exploring the package documentation in the callout above too.

title: 4  Cleaning Data
text:
4.3 lubridate

4.3.1 Working with Dates
Earlier in the book we covered readr’s parsing functions for reading in dates. readr is great, but there is a package whose only job is to work with dates and it makes incredibly ergonomical and intuitive.
You may have noticed that the last_update_date column in our covid_clean isn’t considered a date in R, but rather a character string. If you’re not going to be manipulating the dates, this isn’t a problem. However, if you want to do any date math - such as calculating the number of days between two dates, or filtering for dates within a certain range - you’ll need to convert the character string to a date object.
Take a look at last_update_date:

covid_clean |>
  select(last_update_date) |> # select ONLY this column
  slice(1:5) # slice the first 5 rows - kind of like head()

# A tibble: 5 × 1
  last_update_date
  <chr>           
1 06/24/2022      
2 06/24/2022      
3 06/24/2022      
4 06/24/2022      
5 06/24/2022      


Date format jargon is easy to lose track of, and with lubridate you don’t have to remember it. Those dates look like the month, then the day, then the year.
We will tell lubridate that the date is in the month-day-year format by using its mdy() function and it handles the rest.

# we are going to change the character string to a date and then save the changes
# back to itself

covid_clean <-
  covid_clean |>
  mutate(last_update_date = mdy(last_update_date)) # mutate for manipulating columns

covid_clean |>
  select(last_update_date) |>
  slice(1:5)

# A tibble: 5 × 1
  last_update_date
  <date>          
1 2022-06-24      
2 2022-06-24      
3 2022-06-24      
4 2022-06-24      
5 2022-06-24      


Did you catch the <date> below the column name in the output? It is a date now and can be seen in R’s standard date format. We can now do date operations on this column.
We can do simple things like this…

# how many days are in the dataset?
max(covid_clean$last_update_date) - min(covid_clean$last_update_date)

Time difference of 822 days


or more complex things like this…

# average total deaths per calendar week - demonstration purposes only

covid_clean |>
  group_by(week = floor_date(last_update_date, "week")) |> # here we are using lubridate's floor_date() to round down to the nearest week
  summarise(avg_total_deaths = mean(total_deaths, na.rm = TRUE)) |> # here we are using dplyr's summarise() to calculate the average total deaths per week
  slice(1:5)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  week       avg_total_deaths
  <date>                <dbl>
1 2020-03-22            0.118
2 2020-03-29            0.530
3 2020-04-05            1.95 
4 2020-04-12            4.87 
5 2020-04-19            9.01 


mdy() isn’t the only parser in the family. lubridate has a parsing function for every common date order - the function name spells out the order of year (y), month (m), and day (d) that it expects in the string:

ymd("2026-06-30")

[1] "2026-06-30"

mdy("06/30/2026")

[1] "2026-06-30"

dmy("30-06-2026")

[1] "2026-06-30"


Pick whichever one matches the order used in your source data - no format string, no strptime codes to look up.
It is important to keep in mind what folks want to do with these data and then clean them in a manner that will make it easier to do those things.


4.3.2 Converting to dates with as_date()
Sometimes a column is already a date-time (POSIXct), with hours, minutes, and seconds attached, but the analysis only needs the calendar date. as_date() truncates it:

now() # a datetime, with a time attached

[1] "2026-07-24 15:18:18 EDT"

now() |> as_date() # a calendar date, time dropped

[1] "2026-07-24"




4.3.3 Pulling out the day of the week with wday()
CT DPH published new case counts on a schedule, and gaps or slowdowns in reporting often line up with weekends. wday() extracts the day of the week from a date, and label = TRUE gives you a readable name instead of a number:

covid_clean |>
  distinct(last_update_date) |>
  mutate(day_of_week = wday(last_update_date, label = TRUE)) |>
  count(day_of_week)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  day_of_week     n
  <ord>       <int>
1 Sun            57
2 Mon           112
3 Tue           118
4 Wed           117
5 Thu           115
6 Fri            72
7 Sat            14


That count is a quick way to check whether report dates cluster on certain days of the week - useful for spotting reporting cadence, or gaps, before you build anything downstream that assumes daily data.






TipThe lubridate family, at a glance










Function
What it does




ymd(), mdy(), dmy()
Parse a character string into a date, given the order of year/month/day


as_date()
Convert a datetime (POSIXct) down to a calendar date


wday(x, label = TRUE)
Extract the day of the week as a name


floor_date(x, "week")
Round a date down to the start of its week

title: 4  Cleaning Data
text:
4.4 tidyr
tidyr is a wonderful package for creating and reshaping tidy data.
Pivoting data is a common usecase for tidyr. Our covid_clean dataset as-is, is probably fine for most usecases. However, it was not uncommon for similar data to be presented in a wider format during the pandemic. Let’s purposely un-tidy our data by making it wide and use the town names as the column names, something that should be a value in the data. We will then take our wide ‘messy’ data and make it tidy again in a longer format.

4.4.1 Reshaping with pivot_wider() and pivot_longer()
pivot_wider() takes a longer dataset and makes it wider.

wide <-
  covid_clean |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = last_update_date, # this uniquely identifies each row in the dataset
    names_from = town, # think to yourself, "what do I want to use as the new column names?"
    values_from = total_cases, # think to yourself, "what do I want to use as the values in the new columns?"
    names_prefix = "cases_"
  ) |>
  clean_names()

wide |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 170
  last_update_date cases_andover cases_ansonia cases_ashford cases_avon
  <date>                   <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>
1 2022-06-24                 514          4911           744       3030
2 2022-06-23                 512          4904           744       3020
3 2022-06-22                 512          4900           742       3015
4 2022-06-21                 512          4898           742       3010
5 2022-06-20                 511          4892           741       3005
6 2022-06-17                 506          4887           738       2999
# ℹ 165 more variables: cases_barkhamsted <dbl>, cases_beacon_falls <dbl>,
#   cases_berlin <dbl>, cases_bethany <dbl>, cases_bethel <dbl>,
#   cases_bethlehem <dbl>, cases_bloomfield <dbl>, cases_bolton <dbl>,
#   cases_bozrah <dbl>, cases_branford <dbl>, cases_bridgeport <dbl>,
#   cases_bridgewater <dbl>, cases_bristol <dbl>, cases_brookfield <dbl>,
#   cases_brooklyn <dbl>, cases_burlington <dbl>, cases_canaan <dbl>,
#   cases_canterbury <dbl>, cases_canton <dbl>, cases_chaplin <dbl>, …


Goodness - that is a lot of columns!
Now let’s take that wide dataset and make it long again.

long <-
  wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !last_update_date, # pivot everything BUT last_update_date. You can also use a helper: starts_with("cases_")
    names_to = "town", # this is the name of the new column that will contain the town names
    values_to = "total_cases" # this is the name of the new column that will contain the total cases
  )

long |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  last_update_date town               total_cases
  <date>           <chr>                    <dbl>
1 2022-06-24       cases_andover              514
2 2022-06-24       cases_ansonia             4911
3 2022-06-24       cases_ashford              744
4 2022-06-24       cases_avon                3030
5 2022-06-24       cases_barkhamsted          527
6 2022-06-24       cases_beacon_falls        1306




4.4.2 Handling missing values with drop_na() and replace_na()
Not every column was filled in from day one. Early in the pandemic, CT DPH hadn’t started splitting cases into confirmed vs. probable yet - confirmed_cases and probable_cases are NA for the earliest reports.

covid_clean |>
  summarise(missing_confirmed = sum(is.na(confirmed_cases)))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  missing_confirmed
              <int>
1             11492


That’s a real gap, not a typo, and you have two honest ways to handle it depending on what comes next.
drop_na() removes rows missing a given column - use it when an analysis genuinely needs the confirmed/probable breakdown and rows without it can’t contribute:

covid_clean |>
  drop_na(confirmed_cases) |>
  nrow()

[1] 90753


replace_na() keeps every row and fills the gap with a value you choose:

covid_clean |>
  replace_na(list(confirmed_cases = 0, probable_cases = 0)) |>
  select(last_update_date, confirmed_cases, probable_cases) |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  last_update_date confirmed_cases probable_cases
  <date>                     <dbl>          <dbl>
1 2022-06-24                   439             75
2 2022-06-24                  4222            689
3 2022-06-24                   671             73
4 2022-06-24                  2773            257
5 2022-06-24                   490             37
6 2022-06-24                  1163            143








Warning



Filling NA with 0 says “this was measured, and the answer was zero.” That’s not what happened here - the confirmed/probable split simply wasn’t being tracked yet. Replacing with 0 would make early 2020 look like it had zero confirmed cases, which is misleading in a public health report. drop_na() or leaving the NA in place is usually the more honest choice; only reach for replace_na() when missing genuinely does mean the same thing as zero (or whatever value you’re filling in with).




4.4.3 Splitting and combining columns with separate() and unite()
Sometimes several pieces of information need to travel together in one column - a “2026-06” style label for grouping by month, for example. unite() glues columns together with a separator:

dates_split <-
  covid_clean |>
  mutate(
    report_year = year(last_update_date),
    report_month = month(last_update_date)
  ) |>
  select(last_update_date, report_year, report_month) |>
  distinct()

dates_united <-
  dates_split |>
  unite(col = "year_month", report_year, report_month, sep = "-", remove = FALSE)

dates_united |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  last_update_date year_month report_year report_month
  <date>           <chr>            <dbl>        <dbl>
1 2022-06-24       2022-6            2022            6
2 2022-06-23       2022-6            2022            6
3 2022-06-22       2022-6            2022            6
4 2022-06-21       2022-6            2022            6
5 2022-06-20       2022-6            2022            6
6 2022-06-17       2022-6            2022            6


separate() does the reverse - split one column into several using a separator to know where to break it apart:

dates_united |>
  select(last_update_date, year_month) |>
  separate(col = year_month, into = c("year", "month"), sep = "-") |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  last_update_date year  month
  <date>           <chr> <chr>
1 2022-06-24       2022  6    
2 2022-06-23       2022  6    
3 2022-06-22       2022  6    
4 2022-06-21       2022  6    
5 2022-06-20       2022  6    
6 2022-06-17       2022  6    


Just like the wide/long round trip earlier, unite() and separate() are inverses of each other - whichever shape a report or a join needs, the other function gets you back.

title: 4  Cleaning Data
text:
4.5 stringr and glue
Public health data is full of free text - town names, facility names, notes fields, category labels typed by different people at different times. stringr gives you consistent functions for detecting, replacing, and reshaping that text. glue turns data into sentences, useful for report text, labels, and messages that need to fill in with real values from your dataset instead of being copy-pasted by hand.

4.5.1 Detecting patterns with str_detect()
str_detect() returns TRUE/FALSE for whether a pattern appears in each string. Use it inside filter() to keep only rows that match.

covid_clean |>
  distinct(town) |>
  filter(str_detect(town, "New"))

# A tibble: 9 × 1
  town         
  <chr>        
1 New Britain  
2 New Canaan   
3 New Fairfield
4 New Hartford 
5 New Haven    
6 Newington    
7 New London   
8 New Milford  
9 Newtown      


That caught more than towns actually named “New Something” - Newington and Newtown matched too, because str_detect() looks for the pattern anywhere in the string. Anchor the pattern to the start with ^ and require a space after “New” to match only the compound names:

covid_clean |>
  distinct(town) |>
  filter(str_detect(town, "^New "))

# A tibble: 7 × 1
  town         
  <chr>        
1 New Britain  
2 New Canaan   
3 New Fairfield
4 New Hartford 
5 New Haven    
6 New London   
7 New Milford  




4.5.2 Changing case with str_to_title() and friends
Data entered by hand rarely agrees on case. str_to_upper(), str_to_lower(), and str_to_title() normalize it:

"HARTFORD" |> str_to_title()

[1] "Hartford"

"hartford" |> str_to_upper()

[1] "HARTFORD"

"Hartford" |> str_to_lower()

[1] "hartford"


Reach for str_to_title() when preparing labels for a plot or report where you want consistent, presentable capitalization no matter how the value happened to be stored.


4.5.3 Trimming whitespace with str_trim()
Stray leading or trailing whitespace is invisible in a viewer but breaks joins and comparisons. str_trim() removes it:

"  Hartford   " |> str_trim()

[1] "Hartford"


If a filter() or a join isn’t matching rows you know should match, whitespace like this is one of the first things worth checking.


4.5.4 Replacing values with str_replace()
str_replace() swaps the first match of a pattern; str_replace_all() swaps every match. Both take the same three arguments: the string, the pattern to find, and the replacement.

covid_clean |>
  distinct(town) |>
  filter(str_detect(town, "^New ")) |>
  mutate(short_name = str_replace(town, "^New ", "N. "))

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  town          short_name  
  <chr>         <chr>       
1 New Britain   N. Britain  
2 New Canaan    N. Canaan   
3 New Fairfield N. Fairfield
4 New Hartford  N. Hartford 
5 New Haven     N. Haven    
6 New London    N. London   
7 New Milford   N. Milford  




4.5.5 Building sentences with glue()
glue() interpolates R values directly into a string. Wrap any expression in {} and it is evaluated and inserted in place:

town_name <- "Hartford"

case_count <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(town == town_name, last_update_date == max(last_update_date)) |>
  pull(total_cases)

glue("As of the latest report, {town_name} had {case_count} total cases.")

As of the latest report, Hartford had 33844 total cases.


glue() also works row-by-row against a data frame column, which is the more common way you’ll use it in practice:

covid_clean |>
  filter(last_update_date == max(last_update_date)) |>
  slice(1:3) |>
  mutate(
    summary = glue("{town}: {total_cases} total cases, {total_deaths} deaths")
  ) |>
  pull(summary)

Andover: 514 total cases, 6 deaths
Ansonia: 4911 total cases, 49 deaths
Ashford: 744 total cases, 5 deaths


This is the kind of line that goes straight into an automated report - no manually copying numbers into a sentence, and no risk of a stale number left over from last week’s version.

title: 6  Building a Dataset
text:
6.1 The plan
Every dataset so far has been a count table: one row per town per report date, with cumulative cases and deaths. That’s what the state publishes, and it’s plenty for trends and maps. But a lot of everyday epi work happens one level down — at the case level. How old were the people who got sick? How long between symptom onset and a positive report? What share of hospitalized patients died, and did that differ by age?
None of those questions can be answered from a count table, because the individual people have already been summed away. To practice case-level work you need a line-list: one row per case, with that person’s age, dates, and outcomes.
Real line-lists exist — but they’re confidential. You can’t paste real patients into a public book. So this chapter does the next best thing: it manufactures a fake line-list from the real counts, and the act of building it is the lesson. It also means stepping away from the town-level Commissioner briefing for a chapter or two — the real town data resumes in the Data Visualization chapter — while we drop down to the case level, where a safe-to-share synthetic dataset is the only honest option. Along the way you’ll expand a count table into individual rows, invent plausible values with controlled randomness, recode and categorize variables, and do arithmetic on dates — the core moves of data manipulation.
We’ll scope the work to Hartford County during the winter 2020–2021 surge (December 2020 through January 2021) — a real wave, before vaccines were widely available, and a chunk of data small enough to build on a laptop. The recipe has three moves:

title: 6  Building a Dataset
text:
Start from the real town counts and work out how many new cases each town had on each report date.
Expand those counts into one row per case.
Attach invented-but-plausible demographics and outcomes to each row.

title: 6  Building a Dataset
section: 6.2 Part A — How the line-list was built
text:
6.2 Part A — How the line-list was built
The full recipe lives in data-raw/make-synthetic-linelist.R in the book’s repository. We’ll walk through it a piece at a time. You don’t need to run it yourself — the finished file is in the Data Library — but reading it teaches the moves.

6.2.1 Real counts into new cases
Total cases is cumulative, so a town’s new cases on a given day are the change from its previous report — the same lag() trick from earlier chapters. We floor negatives at zero (the state sometimes revises an old total downward, and you can’t have negative people), then keep only our county and our two-month window.

hartford_county <- c(
  "Avon",
  "Berlin",
  "Bloomfield",
  "Bristol",
  "Burlington",
  "Canton",
  "East Granby",
  "East Hartford",
  "East Windsor",
  "Enfield",
  "Farmington",
  "Glastonbury",
  "Granby",
  "Hartford",
  "Hartland",
  "Manchester",
  "Marlborough",
  "New Britain",
  "Newington",
  "Plainville",
  "Rocky Hill",
  "Simsbury",
  "Southington",
  "South Windsor",
  "Suffield",
  "West Hartford",
  "Wethersfield",
  "Windsor",
  "Windsor Locks"
)

counts <-
  read_csv(here("data", "raw", "ct_covid_by_town_2026-06-30.csv")) |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    report_date = mdy(last_update_date),
    town = str_to_title(str_trim(town)),
    total_cases = parse_number(as.character(total_cases))
  ) |>
  filter(town %in% hartford_county) |>
  arrange(town, report_date) |>
  group_by(town) |>
  mutate(new_cases = total_cases - lag(total_cases)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(new_cases = pmax(new_cases, 0)) |>
  filter(
    report_date >= as.Date("2020-12-01"),
    report_date <= as.Date("2021-01-31"),
    !is.na(new_cases),
    new_cases > 0
  ) |>
  select(town, report_date, new_cases)

That leaves a compact table: for each town and report date, how many new cases showed up. Now we blow it apart.


6.2.2 One row per case with uncount()
tidyr::uncount() is the workhorse of this chapter. Hand it a column of counts and it repeats each row that many times — the exact inverse of count(). A row that says “Hartford, 2020-12-15, 90 new cases” becomes 90 identical Hartford rows.

linelist <- counts |>
  uncount(new_cases) |>
  mutate(case_id = sprintf("HC-%06d", row_number()))

Each row is now one case. They’re still identical within a town-day, so the last step is to give each one an identity.


6.2.3 Inventing values with set.seed() and random draws
To fill in age, sex, and the rest we draw values at random from distributions we pick. sample() draws from a set of categories with given probabilities; rnorm() draws numbers from a bell curve; rbinom() flips weighted coins (hospitalized or not, died or not).
Random draws are different every time you run them — which would make the dataset impossible to reproduce. set.seed() fixes the random number generator so every draw comes out the same on every run. Set it once, at the top, before any drawing happens.

set.seed(20210101)







NoteA cleaner seed is coming later



set.seed() changes the random state for the rest of your session, which is fine in a one-shot script like this but can surprise you in a longer analysis. The reproducibility chapter will introduce withr::with_seed(), which sets a seed for just one expression and then puts the random state back the way it found it — the tidier tool when you only want one block of code to be reproducible. For a standalone data-generation script, plain set.seed() at the top is perfectly good.


With the seed fixed, every field is one mutate() away. A few patterns worth naming:

A number from a distribution — age from a bell curve centered on 42, clamped to a human range with pmin()/pmax():
age = pmin(pmax(round(rnorm(n, mean = 42, sd = 22)), 0L), 100L)
A category with set odds — sample() with a prob vector. These proportions are illustrative, not measured:
sex = sample(c("Female", "Male"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.51, 0.49))
A weighted coin flip that depends on another column — case_when() builds an age-dependent probability, then rbinom() flips it. Hospitalization risk climbs steeply with age:
hosp_prob = case_when(
  age < 18 ~ 0.01,
  age < 50 ~ 0.02,
  age < 65 ~ 0.06,
  age < 80 ~ 0.15,
  TRUE     ~ 0.30
)
hospitalized = if_else(rbinom(n, 1, hosp_prob) == 1, "Yes", "No")
A date relative to another date — onset happens a few days before the report; subtract a random number of days:
onset_date = report_date - sample(3:14, n, replace = TRUE)

The full script layers a handful of these together, drops the intermediate probability columns, and writes the result with write_csv(). That’s the whole trick: real counts decide how many rows, random draws decide what’s in them.

6.3 Part B — Working with the line-list

The twelve columns:



Column
What it is

Everything below runs on this real (fake) data.

6.3.1 Categorizing a continuous variable
Age as a raw number is hard to tabulate — you rarely want a row for every single year. Collapsing it into groups is a job for case_when(), reading top to bottom and stopping at the first match:

linelist <- linelist |>
  mutate(
    age_group = case_when(
      age < 18 ~ "0-17",
      age < 50 ~ "18-49",
      age < 65 ~ "50-64",
      age < 80 ~ "65-79",
      TRUE ~ "80+"
    )
  )

count(linelist, age_group)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  age_group     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 0-17       4602
2 18-49     17627
3 50-64      7579
4 65-79      3885
5 80+        1529




6.3.2 Recoding values
hospitalized and died arrived as "Yes"/"No" text. For counting that’s fine, but for modelling later you’ll often want a clean logical. if_else() recodes a single variable in one line:

linelist <- linelist |>
  mutate(
    hospitalized_flag = if_else(hospitalized == "Yes", TRUE, FALSE),
    died_flag = if_else(died == "Yes", TRUE, FALSE)
  )

count(linelist, hospitalized, hospitalized_flag)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  hospitalized hospitalized_flag     n
  <chr>        <lgl>             <int>
1 No           FALSE             33319
2 Yes          TRUE               1903




6.3.3 Doing arithmetic on dates
Subtracting one date from another gives a number of days. Two classic epi measures fall straight out of that:

Reporting delay — how long from symptom onset to the case being reported.
Length of stay — how long a hospitalized patient was admitted.


linelist <- linelist |>
  mutate(
    reporting_delay = as.integer(report_date - onset_date),
    length_of_stay = as.integer(hosp_discharge_date - hosp_admit_date)
  )

linelist |>
  summarise(
    median_delay = median(reporting_delay),
    median_stay = median(length_of_stay, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2

1            8          12


length_of_stay is NA for anyone who was never admitted, which is exactly right — there’s no stay to measure. That’s why na.rm = TRUE is needed in the summary.


6.3.4 Selecting a date range
Filtering to a window is the same filter() you already know, with date comparisons. Say you only want cases reported in the first two weeks of December:

linelist |>
  filter(
    report_date >= as.Date("2020-12-01"),
    report_date <= as.Date("2020-12-14")
  ) |>
  nrow()

[1] 9409




6.3.5 A quick sanity check
Before trusting any built dataset, look for values that can’t be real. Ages should sit between 0 and about 120; onset should never come after the report. A filter() that returns zero rows is a clean bill of health:

linelist |>
  filter(age < 0 | age > 120 | onset_date > report_date) |>
  nrow()

[1] 0


Zero out-of-range rows — no surprise, since we built the data to behave, but on real data this is the check that catches a birth year of 1850 or a typo’d date.


6.3.6 Does it match the real counts?
The whole point of anchoring to real data is that the totals should line up. The synthetic line-list has one row per real case in the window, so its row count equals the real number of new cases Hartford County recorded from December 2020 through January 2021:

text:
6.4 Wrap-up
You started with a published count table and ended with a case-level line-list you can slice by age, date, and outcome. More importantly you practiced the manipulation moves that show up everywhere: uncount() to go from counts to rows, case_when() to recode and categorize, seeded random draws to fill in values reproducibly, and date arithmetic to turn two dates into a meaningful number. The next chapters lean on exactly these skills — now on data that finally has a person in every row.






Note



The finished file, its source page, and the generator script are cataloged in the Data Library.

title: 7  Describing and Testing
text:
7.1 Getting set up
You built a line-list in the last chapter — one row per case, with an age, a set of dates, and outcome flags. Now we get to ask questions of it. This chapter is the everyday inferential toolkit: describe what’s in the data, cross-tabulate one variable against another, and run the handful of statistical tests that answer “is this pattern real, or could it be chance?”
If you’re coming from SAS, this is PROC FREQ and PROC MEANS territory — just tidier, and with the whole thing scriptable end to end.
We’ll lean on two packages: dplyr for the summarising and janitor for the epi-friendly tables. In your own covid-briefing/ project you’d start by reading the file you built:
linelist <- read_csv(here("data", "synthetic-covid-linelist.csv"))
Then we recreate the age_group column from the previous chapter — most of the questions in this chapter are about how outcomes vary across ages, and a handful of ordered bands is far easier to tabulate than raw years:
library(dplyr)
library(janitor)

linelist <- linelist |>
  mutate(
    age_group = case_when(
      age < 18 ~ "0-17",
      age < 50 ~ "18-49",
      age < 65 ~ "50-64",
      age < 80 ~ "65-79",
      TRUE     ~ "80+"
    )
  )

title: 7  Describing and Testing
text:
7.2 Section 1 — Describing what you have
Before any test, look at the data. The first question about almost any outcome is simply how often did it happen? — counts and percents.
janitor::tabyl() is the tool for that. Hand it a column and it returns a tidy table of counts and proportions; adorn_pct_formatting() turns the raw proportions into readable percentages. If you’ve reached for PROC FREQ in SAS, this is the same job.

linelist |>
  tabyl(died) |>
  adorn_pct_formatting()

 died     n percent
   No 34316   97.4%
  Yes   906    2.6%


That’s your case fatality snapshot: about 2.6% of cases in this line-list died. tabyl() is a data frame like any other, so it drops straight into a report or a gt table later without any wrestling.
Counts answer “how many.” For a continuous variable like age you want the shape — where the middle sits and how far it spreads. summarise() gives you whichever statistics you name, and the classic epi move is to compute them split by outcome so you can compare. Here’s “does age differ between people who died and people who survived?”:

linelist |>
  group_by(died) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_age   = round(mean(age), 1),
    median_age = median(age),
    min_age    = min(age),
    max_age    = max(age)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  died      n mean_age median_age min_age max_age
  <chr> <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 No    34316     41.4         41       0     100
2 Yes     906     74.8         79       0     100


Read across the two rows and the story jumps out. Among the people who died, the mean age is about 74.8 and the median 79; among survivors the mean is 41.4 and the median 41. Deaths skew old — decades older, on average. The mean and median sitting close together within each group also tells you neither is being dragged around by a few extreme outliers.
This one table is often the whole descriptive section of a briefing. But it also raises the obvious follow-up: we can see that deaths are older, but is the association between age and death strong enough to trust? That’s what the next section is for.

title: 7  Describing and Testing
section: 7.3 Section 2 — Cross-tabulation with a statistical test
text:
7.3 Section 2 — Cross-tabulation with a statistical test
The natural next step is a two-way table: age group down the side, outcome across the top. tabyl() takes two variables and builds exactly that, and the adorn_* helpers layer on the pieces you want to see.

linelist |>
  tabyl(age_group, died) |>
  adorn_totals("row") |>
  adorn_percentages("row") |>
  adorn_pct_formatting() |>
  adorn_ns()

 age_group             No         Yes
      0-17 99.9%  (4,598)  0.1%   (4)
     18-49 99.5% (17,542)  0.5%  (85)
     50-64 98.8%  (7,491)  1.2%  (88)
     65-79 92.8%  (3,604)  7.2% (281)
       80+ 70.7%  (1,081) 29.3% (448)
     Total 97.4% (34,316)  2.6% (906)


There’s a lot packed into that pipe, so here’s what each adornment does:

adorn_totals("row") adds a totals row across the bottom.
adorn_percentages("row") converts each cell to a row percentage — so each age group’s numbers add to 100% across its own row.
adorn_pct_formatting() formats those as percents.
adorn_ns() puts the raw counts back in, in parentheses, so you never lose sight of how many people each percentage rests on.

Why row percents? Because the row is the age group, so the percentage in the Yes column is the case fatality rate within that age group — exactly the number an epidemiologist wants. Reading down that Yes column, the CFR climbs steadily: roughly 0.1% for 0–17, 0.5% for 18–49, 1.2% for 50–64, 7.2% for 65–79, and 29.3% for the 80+ group. Nearly three in ten of the oldest cases died. That’s the association from Section 1, now resolved group by group.
Seeing a trend in a table and establishing it statistically are two different things. A chi-square test asks whether the association between age group and outcome could plausibly have arisen by chance if the two were actually unrelated.

age_died <- table(linelist$age_group, linelist$died)
chisq.test(age_died)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  age_died
X-squared = 5176.2, df = 4, p-value < 2.2e-16


table() builds the plain contingency table (chi-square wants counts, not percentages), and chisq.test() does the rest. The null hypothesis is that there is no association — that outcome doesn’t depend on age group. The test returns a huge X-squared statistic (around 5176) on 4 degrees of freedom and a p-value below 2.2e-16, which is R’s way of printing “smaller than I bother to show.” In plain terms: if age and death were truly unrelated, a table this lopsided would essentially never happen. We reject the null.






WarningA tiny p-value is not a big effect



With this many cases, almost any association will come back “significant” — the p-value is partly a measure of your sample size. A huge n makes the test exquisitely sensitive, so it will flag even trivial differences. Don’t let a row of zeros after the decimal point fool you into thinking you’ve found something important. The effect size — the actual jump from 0.1% to 29.3% CFR you read off the cross-tab — is what makes this finding matter. The p-value only tells you it’s not noise; the percentages tell you it’s a big deal.



7.3.1 When cells are small: Fisher’s exact test
Chi-square relies on an approximation that gets shaky when the expected count in any cell is small — the usual rule of thumb is that no expected cell should drop below 5. That happens all the time when you slice down to a single small town or a rare outcome. Fisher’s exact test computes the exact probability instead of approximating it, so it stays honest on sparse tables.
Let’s force the situation by looking at one small town, Hartland:

hartland <- linelist |> filter(town == "Hartland")

table(hartland$hospitalized, hartland$died)

     
      No Yes
  No  56   0
  Yes  1   2

fisher.test(table(hartland$hospitalized, hartland$died))


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  table(hartland$hospitalized, hartland$died)
p-value = 0.001753
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 4.415925      Inf
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
       Inf 


Hartland has only 59 cases, and the table() shows why chi-square would struggle: the cells are thin and at least one is a flat zero. fisher.test() handles that without complaint and returns a p-value of about 0.0018 — strong evidence of an association between being hospitalized and dying, even in this tiny slice.
The teaching point: reach for Fisher when the counts are small. If you run chisq.test() on a sparse table it’ll warn you that the approximation may be unreliable — that warning is your cue to switch. On small or zero-heavy tables, Fisher is the trustworthy choice.

title: 7  Describing and Testing
section: 7.4 Section 3 — Testing a trend in proportions
text:
7.4 Section 3 — Testing a trend in proportions
The stakeholder didn’t just ask “is there an association” — they asked about trends in proportions, like an outcome rising over time or across ordered categories. A plain chi-square treats the age groups as unordered labels; it would give the same answer if you shuffled them. But our age bands have a natural order, and the interesting claim is specifically that CFR rises monotonically from young to old.
The test for trend in proportions (a Cochran–Armitage-style test) is built for that. It needs two things in order: the number of deaths in each group, and the number of cases in each group. We build those with a grouped summarise(), then arrange() to lock in the order:

cfr_by_age <-
  linelist |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(died == "Yes"), n = n()) |>
  arrange(age_group)

cfr_by_age

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  age_group deaths     n
  <chr>      <int> <int>
1 0-17           4  4602
2 18-49         85 17627
3 50-64         88  7579
4 65-79        281  3885
5 80+          448  1529

prop.trend.test(cfr_by_age$deaths, cfr_by_age$n)


    Chi-squared Test for Trend in Proportions

data:  cfr_by_age$deaths out of cfr_by_age$n ,
 using scores: 1 2 3 4 5
X-squared = 2918.6, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16


sum(died == "Yes") counts the deaths in each group (a TRUE/FALSE vector sums to the number of TRUEs), and n() counts everyone. prop.trend.test() takes the deaths and the group sizes and asks: is there a directional trend in the proportion across these ordered groups?
The result — X-squared around 2919 on 1 degree of freedom, p below 2.2e-16 — says yes, emphatically: CFR increases in a clear linear fashion across the age bands. Because this test uses the ordering of the groups, it’s a sharper instrument than a plain chi-square when the order is meaningful. It’s asking a more specific question (“does it trend?”) and so gives stronger evidence when the answer is yes.
The same machinery answers the stakeholder’s “outcome by year” question directly: group by year instead of age band, feed the yearly death counts and case counts into prop.trend.test() in chronological order, and you’re testing whether the outcome trended up or down over time. Any ordered grouping — age bands, years, weeks of a wave — works the same way.

title: 7  Describing and Testing
text:
7.5 Wrap-up
You can now do the three things that make up the bread-and-butter of case-level analysis: describe a line-list with counts and summaries, cross-tabulate two variables and test the association with chi-square or Fisher’s exact test, and test a trend across ordered groups. That’s the everyday inferential toolkit, and it’ll carry you through most routine surveillance questions.
What it won’t do is untangle variables that move together. Older cases might also be more likely to be hospitalized, or to belong to a particular group — and these simple tests look at one relationship at a time. The next chapter, Modeling, is how you get adjusted effect estimates that hold age, sex, and the rest constant all at once.






Note



Want this chapter’s work as a runnable script? See project-snapshots/line-list-practice on GitHub. 02_describe_and_test.R is the script version of everything above — the tabyls, the chi-square, Fisher’s, and the trend test — ready to drop into your scripts/ folder.

title: 8  Modeling: Adjusted Effect Estimates
text:
8.1 From cross-tab to model
The previous chapter left you with a cliffhanger. Your cross-tabs showed two clear things: case fatality climbs steeply with age, and — separately — hospitalized cases die far more often than non-hospitalized ones. Both are real signals. But they’re tangled together. Older people are also the ones most likely to be hospitalized, so when you look at hospitalization and death in a cross-tab, some of what you’re seeing is really just age wearing a different hat.
A two-way table can’t pull those apart. It only ever looks at one relationship at a time. What you need is a way to ask: what is the effect of age on death, holding hospitalization and sex constant? And at the same time, what is the effect of hospitalization, holding age and sex constant? That “holding the others constant” is exactly what a regression does, and it’s exactly what a stakeholder means when they ask for adjusted effect estimates.
This chapter fits a logistic regression — the workhorse model for a yes/no outcome like died — and reads the results as odds ratios with confidence intervals. If this is your first model in R, don’t worry: we’ll take it a piece at a time and translate every number into a plain sentence.
The previous chapter’s tools — chi-square, Fisher’s, the trend test — each answer a question about one pair of variables. Regression answers a different kind of question: given several predictors at once, what does each one contribute on its own? The model estimates every effect net of the others, which is the whole point. When it tells you the odds ratio for age, that number already has hospitalization and sex accounted for.

title: 8  Modeling: Adjusted Effect Estimates
text:
NoteThis chapter uses broom



We’ll use broom to turn the model’s output into a tidy data frame. It may not be installed yet. In your own covid-briefing/ project, install it once with:
install.packages("broom")
If you’re building this book from its repository (which uses renv), install it into the project library instead and record it in the lockfile:
renv::install("broom")
renv::snapshot()
broom takes the somewhat awkward object that glm() hands back and turns it into a clean, rectangular data frame you can read, filter, and drop into a report — the same shape as everything else you’ve worked with.

title: 8  Modeling: Adjusted Effect Estimates
text:
8.2 Fit a logistic regression
A little prep first. Two small but important setup moves before we fit anything.
First, an ordered age variable with a deliberate reference level. A regression with a categorical predictor doesn’t estimate an effect for every level — it picks one level as the baseline (the “reference”) and reports every other level relative to it. We make age_group a factor and put "18-49" first, which makes it the reference. That’s a choice with meaning: healthy working-age adults are the natural comparison group, so every age odds ratio will read as “compared to a 18–49-year-old.” Reference-first is a habit worth building.
Second, a numeric 0/1 outcome. Logistic regression models the probability of an event happening, so it needs the outcome coded as 1 for the event (died) and 0 for not. Our died column is "Yes"/"No" text; as.integer(died == "Yes") turns it into exactly the 1/0 the model wants.

library(dplyr)
library(broom)

model_data <-
  linelist |>
  mutate(
    age_group = factor(
      case_when(
        age < 18 ~ "0-17",
        age < 50 ~ "18-49",
        age < 65 ~ "50-64",
        age < 80 ~ "65-79",
        TRUE     ~ "80+"
      ),
      levels = c("18-49", "0-17", "50-64", "65-79", "80+")
    ),
    died_flag = as.integer(died == "Yes")
  )

Now the model itself. glm() — generalized linear model — is the function, and the two arguments that make it a logistic regression are the formula and the family.
The formula died_flag ~ age_group + sex + hospitalized reads left to right as “died explained by age group, plus sex, plus hospitalization.” The ~ is “is modeled by”; the + signs add predictors. family = binomial is the piece that makes this logistic: it tells glm() the outcome is a yes/no event and to work on the log-odds scale rather than fitting a straight line.

model <- glm(
  died_flag ~ age_group + sex + hospitalized,
  data = model_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(model)
