There’s a lot there, but the key thing to know right now is that the numbers in the Estimate column are on the log-odds scale. A log-odds coefficient is nearly impossible to read directly — nobody thinks in log-odds. That’s why we almost never stop here. The next step converts these into odds ratios, which you can read.

title: 8  Modeling: Adjusted Effect Estimates
text:
8.3 Odds ratios with broom
Here’s where broom earns its keep. tidy() takes the model and returns a tidy data frame, one row per term. Two arguments do the heavy lifting: exponentiate = TRUE converts those log-odds coefficients into odds ratios, and conf.int = TRUE adds a 95% confidence interval for each one.

tidy(model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 7 × 7
  term            estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>              <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)      0.00450    0.115    -46.9   0          0.00357   0.00560
2 age_group0-17    0.186      0.512     -3.28  1.02e-  3  0.0569    0.447  
3 age_group50-64   2.19       0.153      5.10  3.31e-  7  1.62      2.95   
4 age_group65-79  12.1        0.128     19.5   1.13e- 84  9.44     15.6    
5 age_group80+    55.1        0.127     31.7   5.50e-220 43.2      71.1    
6 sexMale          1.03       0.0750     0.341 7.33e-  1  0.886     1.19   
7 hospitalizedYes  4.10       0.0827    17.1   2.93e- 65  3.49      4.82   


Now every number is legible. The estimate column is the odds ratio, and conf.low/conf.high bracket the 95% CI. Here’s how to read an odds ratio:

Greater than 1 means higher odds of the outcome than the reference.
Less than 1 means lower odds.
Exactly 1 means no difference at all.

And crucially — every one of these is adjusted for the other predictors in the model. Walk the age gradient, each compared to the 18–49 reference group:

age_group0-17: 0.19 (95% CI 0.06–0.45). Children have about a fifth the odds of death of a working-age adult — far lower, which is why the OR sits well below 1.
age_group50-64: 2.19 (1.62–2.95). Roughly double the odds.
age_group65-79: 12.1 (9.44–15.6). Twelve times the odds.
age_group80+: 55.1 (43.2–71.1). Fifty-five times the odds of death of a working-age adult — a dramatic age gradient, and all of it after adjusting for whether the person was hospitalized.

Then the other two predictors:

hospitalizedYes: 4.10 (3.49–4.82). Hospitalized cases have about four times the odds of death — and, importantly, this is the hospitalization effect with age already accounted for. It’s not just older people showing up again in disguise.
sexMale: 1.03 (0.89–1.19). This one is the teaching moment. The odds ratio is a hair above 1, but look at the confidence interval: it runs from 0.89 to 1.19 — it crosses 1.

That last point deserves its own paragraph. When a confidence interval crosses 1, the data can’t distinguish the effect from “no effect at all.” The interval includes odds ratios below 1 (protective) and above 1 (harmful), so you genuinely cannot say which direction, if any, sex pushes the outcome. This is a null adjusted estimate, and it’s a clean, concrete example of one. Contrast it with the previous chapter’s habit of eyeballing a cross-tab and declaring a pattern: here the model gives you a principled way to say “no, there’s nothing to see in this variable” — the interval says so.
A nice sanity check falls out of all this. Remember how the synthetic data was built: with a strong age effect baked in, no sex effect, and a hospitalization bump. The model recovered exactly that structure — a steep age gradient, a null result for sex, a moderate hospitalization effect. When a model reproduces the signal you know is in the data, that’s reassurance about both the model and the data build.






WarningAn odds ratio is not a risk ratio



People often read an odds ratio as if it were a risk ratio (“55× the risk”), but the two only agree when the outcome is rare. For a common outcome the odds ratio exaggerates the risk ratio, sometimes badly. Death is uncommon enough here that the gap is modest, but keep the distinction in mind — say “odds,” not “risk,” when you report an OR.

title: 8  Modeling: Adjusted Effect Estimates
text:
8.4 The tidymodels way
The glm() you just ran is the right tool for this job. When your goal is an explanatory model — you want an interpretable effect estimate, an adjusted odds ratio to hand a stakeholder — plain glm() plus broom is lean, clear, and hard to beat.
There’s another whole ecosystem in the tidyverse for modeling, called tidymodels, and it’s worth knowing where it fits. Its real strength is prediction: when the goal isn’t “explain” but “forecast,” tidymodels gives you train/test splits, resampling, hyperparameter tuning, and standardized performance metrics, all with a consistent interface. That’s a different job from what we did above.
But two of tidymodels’ habits are worth borrowing even for an explanatory model: recipes for declaring your preprocessing once, and parsnip for a model spec you can re-point at a different engine without rewriting. Here’s the same logistic regression, expressed the tidymodels way. We’re showing it as a reference — it does not run when the book builds — so you can read the shape of it without needing tidymodels installed:

library(recipes)
library(parsnip)
library(workflows)

# died as a factor outcome for classification; first level is the reference
model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(died = factor(died, levels = c("No", "Yes")))

# 1. recipe: declare outcome + predictors and preprocessing (dummy-code factors)
death_recipe <-
  recipe(died ~ age_group + sex + hospitalized, data = model_data) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

# 2. parsnip spec: logistic regression via the glm engine
death_spec <-
  logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm")

# 3. workflow bundles preprocessing + model and fits in one place
death_fit <-
  workflow() |>
  add_recipe(death_recipe) |>
  add_model(death_spec) |>
  fit(data = model_data)

# same tidy odds-ratio table, now from the workflow
tidy(death_fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

What each piece buys you:

recipes — reproducible preprocessing, declared once and reused. Here it’s just dummy-coding the factors, but the same idea scales: step_other() to collapse rare categories into an “other” bucket, step_normalize() to center and scale continuous predictors, and dozens more. You write the recipe once and every fit and prediction uses the identical steps.
parsnip — one model spec, swappable engines. logistic_reg() is the kind of model; set_engine("glm") picks the implementation. Want a penalized version instead? Swap in set_engine("glmnet") and you don’t rewrite the fit.
workflows — bundle the recipe and the model together so they can’t drift apart. The preprocessing and the model travel as one object, which is a genuine reproducibility win on a bigger project.

When should you actually reach for full tidymodels? When the goal is prediction. That’s when you’ll add rsample for train/test splits and cross-validation, and yardstick for metrics like ROC-AUC and accuracy. For an adjusted odds ratio, though — a single explanatory model you want to interpret — glm() and broom are lighter and clearer, and there’s no prize for over-tooling. The full prediction track lives at https://www.tidymodels.org/.
One gotcha to file away: logistic_reg() needs a factor outcome (not the 0/1 integer glm() wanted), and tidymodels treats the first factor level as the reference — the non-event. That’s why the code above sets the levels as c("No", "Yes") deliberately, so that "Yes" (death) is the event being modeled. Set your factor levels on purpose; don’t let the default alphabetical order decide which outcome you’re predicting.

title: 8  Modeling: Adjusted Effect Estimates
text:
8.5 Wrap-up
You fit a real adjusted model. You took a tangle that a cross-tab couldn’t resolve — is it age, or is it hospitalization? — and got a clean answer for each: an odds ratio, adjusted for the others, with a confidence interval that tells you how much to trust it. You saw a strong effect (age), a moderate one (hospitalization), and a genuinely null one (sex, its CI straddling 1), and you learned to read all three off a single tidy table. And you saw where the tidyverse’s bigger modeling toolkit fits, and where it’s more machine than the job needs.
One honest gap remains. Everything here is about odds — the odds that a known case died. It says nothing about rates in a population: age-adjusted death rates, incidence-rate ratios, the per-100,000 measures that much of surveillance runs on. Those need a population denominator — how many people live in each town and age band — which this book doesn’t have in its data yet. When a denominator dataset lands, a future chapter can take up rate-based measures. Until then, you’ve got the case-level model that answers the stakeholder’s actual question: the adjusted effect estimates.






Note



Want this chapter as a runnable script? See project-snapshots/line-list-practice on GitHub. 03_model_deaths.R is the script version of the logistic regression and odds-ratio table you just built, ready to drop into your scripts/ folder.

title: 9  Visualizing Your Data
text:
9.1 Installing ggplot2
With the synthetic line-list detour behind us, we’re back on the real town-level data and the Commissioner’s briefing.
Earlier we filtered Hartford’s data down to a single tidy tibble. You looked at the rows in your console and we moved on. This is great for getting a feel for the data, but it doesn’t necessarily make it easy to get a feel for how the data change over time.
This chapter teaches you how to turn that tibble into a plot that tells the story to someone else — the Commissioner, a journalist, a colleague who doesn’t want to open a CSV.
ggplot2 gives you a grammar — a language for describing what you want the plot to show, and it handles the drawing.
Before this chapter can work, install the package once.
install.packages("ggplot2")

# You'll also install extra packages later in this chapter for
# mapping and choropleths.
install.packages(c("tigris", "sf"))
Load ggplot2 along with the packages you’ve used so far:
library(ggplot2)

title: 9  Visualizing Your Data
section: 9.2 Building a plot layer by layer
text:
9.2 Building a plot layer by layer

9.2.1 The Grammar of Graphics
ggplot2 is built on a principle called the Grammar of Graphics. It says every plot is made of layers, each adding something to the picture:








Layer
What it does
Example




Data
The tibble to plot
hartford


Aesthetic mapping
Which columns go on which axis, or to color, size, etc.
x = date, y = new_cases


Geometric object
The shape of the marks
dots, lines, bars, areas


Theme
Non-data ink: fonts, backgrounds, axis styling
removal of grid lines, different fonts



Think of it like making a tiered cake. Data are at the bottom - the biggest layer on which everything is built on top of. Aesthetics are next, and then geometry and finally theme is the the very top. ggplot2 code is more or less written in layers, and it is a helpful mental model that will aid you when you reach for ggplot2 for data story telling.






Note



new_cases is the day-over-day change in total_cases — computed with lag() back in the chapter-root setup, not a column that came in the raw file. Chapter 1’s project has the full explanation, including why this number can come out negative on a day the state revises an earlier total.




9.2.2 Your first plot: a scatter plot
We’ll start with the scatter plot.

ggplot(
  data = hartford,
  mapping = aes(
    x = date,
    y = new_cases
  )
) +
  geom_point()








We take our data, our aesthetic and our geometry and we’re already telling stories with those 3 things.
Let’s read them back:

ggplot() starts the plot, supplies the data and the aesthetic mapping (aes) that says “date goes on the x-axis and new_cases goes on the y-axis”.
+ geom_point() adds the layer of dots. The + is what joins layers in ggplot2 — always with a space before and after the +.
Every geometry layer inherits the data and aesthetics from ggplot() unless you override them inside aes() for that specific layer.

The default ggplot2 output works well for internal work, but a briefing needs something cleaner. Let’s build on that first plot.


9.2.3 From dots to a line
Our data is a time-series: date on the x-axis, values on the y-axis. A line makes the trend easier to read.

ggplot(
  data = hartford,
  mapping = aes(
    x = date,
    y = new_cases
  )
) +
  geom_line()








With changing nothing else but the geometry we were able to change the type of plot. This is handy for trying many different kinds of plots with the same data or running different subsets of data through the same geometry to make plots for multiple reports.
This plot still has the default theme’s gray background and the default axis labels read like column names. We’ll work through each of those and make it more presentable.


9.2.4 Title, axis labels, and theme
labs() replaces the automatic labels from column names and adds a title. A theme handles everything that isn’t data — background, gridlines, fonts, axis styling. ggplot2 ships with several, and theme_classic() gets us out of the default gray box and onto something closer to what a briefing slide wants.






TipThemes that come with ggplot2



You don’t have to build a look from scratch. Try swapping these into any plot in this chapter and watch what changes:



Theme
What you get




theme_classic()
White background, axis lines, no gridlines


theme_minimal()
No background, light gridlines, no axis lines


theme_bw()
White background with a full grid and a border


theme_void()
Nothing but the data — useful for maps



Themes stack with + like any other layer, and a later theme() call overrides whatever an earlier theme set.








NoteIf you work at CT DPH



This book renders its own figures with a small set of brand helpers — theme_ct_vertical(), theme_ct_horizontal(), and named palettes like list_ct_primary_colors — so everything matches the DPH brand guide. They aren’t part of ggplot2 and you don’t need them to follow along; the chapter code uses stock themes and plain hex codes so it runs anywhere. If you do have access to them, Further Reading has the full list and how to plug the palettes into ggplot2 scales.



# you can also pipe your data into a plot!

hartford |>
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(
      x = date,
      y = new_cases
    )
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() + # you can add multiple geometries together
  labs(
    title = "New COVID-19 Cases — Hartford",
    subtitle = "Daily count from report to report",
    x = NULL, # use NULL or an empty string "" to remove the x axis title
    y = "New Cases on Each Date"
  ) +
  theme_classic()








x = NULL removes the x-axis label entirely — the title is enough, and everyone reading this knows it shows dates.


9.2.5 Adding color
The default plot line uses the first color in the ggplot2 palette. In public health work you probably want a specific color or branding from your organization.
Map the color aesthetic to a string (a color name) to tint both points and line:

ggplot(data = hartford, mapping = aes(x = date, y = new_cases)) +
  geom_point(color = "#3371E7", size = 2, alpha = 0.1) + # alpha sets the transperancy
  geom_line(color = "#3371E7", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "New COVID-19 Cases — Hartford",
    subtitle = "Daily count from report to report",
    x = NULL,
    y = "New Cases on Each Date",
    caption = "Source: CT DPH COVID-19 open data"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    #inside of theme we can interact with specific plot elements and sub-elements
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50")
  )








Two things to notice:

color = "#3371E7" is set outside aes() because it’s a fixed value, not a column. Inside aes(), R would try to map the literal word “#3371E7” to a legend. You rarely want that.
theme_classic() sets the overall look, then the theme() call after it adjusts two specific pieces. Theme layers stack, and the later one wins wherever they overlap — so reach for a ready-made theme first and only hand-tune what’s left.

That last plot is the kind of thing you’d paste directly into a briefing slide. You built it piece by piece, and each piece does one thing.


9.2.6 Saving the plot
When you’re happy with a plot, save it to outputs/figures/:

ggsave(
  here("outputs", "figures", "hartford_new_cases.png"),
  width = 7,
  height = 4,
  dpi = 300
)

ggsave() saves the last plot you rendered. No need to name it explicitly — just call it immediately after running the plot.

title: 9  Visualizing Your Data
text:
9.3 Aesthetic mapping
So far you’ve been setting the position of the plot (x and y axis). ggplot2 also maps aesthetics to other properties:








Aesthetic
What it controls
Accepts




x, y
Position on the axes
numeric, date, character


color
Stroke/border color of points and line
column name or fixed color


fill
Fill color of bars, areas
column name or fixed color


size
Size of points or line thickness
column name or fixed size


shape
Point shape (0–24 different shapes)
column name or fixed shape


alpha
Transparency (0 = invisible, 1 = opaque)
column name or fixed value


linetype
Dashed, dotted, etc.
column name or fixed value



When you put a column name inside aes(), ggplot2 creates a legend that tells the reader which values map to which colors, sizes, shapes etc. When you set one outside aes(), the value is fixed and no legend is generated.
To see it in action, add a second line to the same plot — one for total_cases (cumulative) — by mapping y to a column:

ggplot(data = hartford, mapping = aes(x = date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = new_cases, color = "New Cases"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = total_cases, color = "Cumulative Cases"), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Metric",
    values = c("New Cases" = "#F27124", "Cumulative Cases" = "#3371E7")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "New Cases vs. Cumulative Cases — Hartford",
    y = "Count",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

title: 9  Visualizing Your Data
text:
9.4 Choropleth maps
A scatter plot shows change over time. A map shows change across space. For a state-level briefing, the Commissioner might want to see case counts across all the towns at once.
The tigris package fetches official boundary files from the Census Bureau. In our case, we want town boundaries for Connecticut:

library(tigris)
library(sf)

# Fetch CT town boundaries
ct_towns <-
  county_subdivisions(
    state = "09",
    cb = TRUE,
    progress_bar = FALSE
  )

# Show just the outlines on a blank canvas
ct_towns |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "gray95", color = "black", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_void() # use this for a blank background








Remember our cake analogy? This is our basemap that we will use to layer additional features on top of.
That’s Connecticut’s 169 towns — just outlines. geom_sf() draws spatial data (the sf geometry column). The rest follows the same pattern as every other ggplot2 plot: ggplot() + geom_sf() + labs() + theme().

9.4.1 Coloring towns by case rate
Now join the COVID data to the map by town name and map fill to the case rate:

# Summarize cases by town on the latest date
latest_date <- max(covid_clean$last_update_date, na.rm = TRUE)

town_cases <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(last_update_date == latest_date) |>
  select(town, case_rate, total_cases)

# Join COVID data to spatial data
ct_bounded <-
  ct_towns |>
  left_join(town_cases, by = join_by(NAME == town))







TipWhat just happened: left_join explained



left_join(x, y, by) keeps every row from the left table (x) and adds matching columns from the right table (y). Where there’s no match, the new columns are filled with NA. Think of it as: “give me all the towns, and bring in any COVID numbers that line up.”
We cover joins in detail in a later chapter — see Further Reading for the full guide.



# Choropleth: gray for towns without data, blue gradient for those with
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = ct_bounded[is.na(ct_bounded$case_rate), ],
    fill = "gray95",
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = ct_bounded[!is.na(ct_bounded$case_rate), ],
    mapping = aes(fill = case_rate),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#C6D4FB",
    mid = "#7094F5",
    high = "#00214D",
    midpoint = mean(ct_bounded$case_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    na.value = "gray95",
    name = "Case Rate\n(per 100,000)"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "COVID-19 Case Rate by Town",
    subtitle = paste("As of", latest_date),
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )








The choropleth tells at a glance which towns carry the heaviest burden. Towns without data (suppressed for small sample sizes) appear gray.






Note



geom_sf() replaces geom_point(), geom_line(), and others when your data is spatial. It reads the geometry column automatically and draws polygons, lines, or points based on the geometry type.








Note



This chapter gave you the foundations of ggplot2 and a taste of spatial visualization. Next up is a quick checkpoint pulling everything together so far, then Managing Code, and eventually functions and API fetching — the full arc from raw data to self-updating report.

title: 10  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
10.1 The fast way: mapview
The choropleth in the last section is built for a slide — you export it once, drop it into a deck, and it doesn’t change again until the next briefing. That’s exactly what a static ggplot2 map is for.
Not every audience gets a slide, though. A web-facing report, an internal dashboard, or an email to a colleague who wants to click around the map themselves calls for something the reader can zoom, pan, and hover over. That’s an interactive map, and R gives you two ways to build one: mapview for a fast look, and leaflet for a map you build and control piece by piece.
Install both once:
mapview(ct_bounded, zcol = "case_rate")
One line. mapview() looks at ct_bounded, sees it’s spatial data, and automatically:
That’s the trade-off: zero setup, but you don’t control any of it. Use mapview() while you’re exploring a dataset at your desk — checking that a join worked, spotting an outlier town, eyeballing a spatial pattern. When you need a specific popup, a specific color ramp, or a specific basemap for a report someone else will read, reach for leaflet instead.

title: 10  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
picks a basemap and drops your polygons on top of it
colors each town by the case_rate column, since you named it in zcol
builds a legend for that column
wires up hover and click popups showing every attribute column

title: 10  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
10.2 The deliberate way: leaflet
leaflet builds a map the same way ggplot2 builds a plot — one piece at a time. Where ggplot2 chains layers with +, leaflet chains them with the pipe. Read a leaflet chain the same way you read a ggplot2 chain: each step adds one thing to the map.

leaflet(ct_bounded) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons()





Three steps:

leaflet(ct_bounded) starts the map and supplies the data — like ggplot(data = ...).
addTiles() adds the basemap (streets, place names) from OpenStreetMap.
addPolygons() draws the town boundaries on top of it.

Right now every town is the same flat blue and tells you nothing. Let’s add the pieces one at a time: popups, then color.

10.2.1 Adding popups
A popup is text that appears when someone clicks (or hovers over, with highlightOptions) a polygon. Build the text yourself with paste0(), one string per town, then pass the whole vector to addPolygons():

town_popup <- paste0(
  "<strong>",
  ct_bounded$NAME,
  "</strong><br/>",
  "Case rate: ",
  round(ct_bounded$case_rate, 1),
  " per 100,000<br/>",
  "Total cases: ",
  ct_bounded$total_cases
)

leaflet(ct_bounded) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(popup = town_popup)





town_popup is a plain character vector, one entry per row of ct_bounded — same length, same order. <strong> and <br/> are HTML tags; leaflet popups render as HTML, so you can bold text and break lines the same way you would on a web page.


10.2.2 Coloring by case rate
colorBin() turns a numeric column into a small palette function — give it bin breaks and colors, and it hands back a function that maps any value in that range to a color. Build the ramp light-to-dark so the map reads the same way the static choropleth did:

case_rate_palette <- colorBin(
  palette = c(
    "#C6D4FB", # lightest
    "#7094F5",
    "#3371E7",
    "#003D9C",
    "#00214D" # darkest
  ),
  domain = ct_bounded$case_rate,
  bins = 5,
  na.color = "gray95"
)

ct_case_map <-
  leaflet(ct_bounded) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~ case_rate_palette(case_rate),
    fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "white",
    weight = 1,
    popup = town_popup
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = case_rate_palette,
    values = ~case_rate,
    title = "Case Rate<br/>(per 100,000)",
    position = "bottomright"
  )

ct_case_map





The lightest blue anchors the low end of the ramp and the darkest anchors the high end — light means fewer cases, dark means more, same logic as scale_fill_gradient2() in the static choropleth. ~case_rate_palette(case_rate) uses leaflet’s formula syntax to say “run this function on the case_rate column of the data I gave leaflet() at the start” — it plays the same role aes(fill = case_rate) played earlier.






Tip



Five hex codes repeated across a dozen plots is five chances to fat-finger one. Once you’re reusing the same ramp, pull the colors into a named object at the top of your script and refer to that instead — change the palette in one place, every plot follows.

title: 10  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
10.3 Marking a single town
You’ve already met Hartford — the daily new-case line chart earlier in this chapter walked through its case counts day by day. A choropleth shows every town at once, but sometimes you want to point a reader at one town in particular. addMarkers() drops a pin at a specific coordinate on top of the map you already built:

ct_case_map |>
  addMarkers(
    lng = -72.6734,
    lat = 41.7658,
    popup = "Hartford — see the daily new-case trend for this town earlier in this chapter."
  )





Piping addMarkers() onto ct_case_map adds the pin without rebuilding the choropleth underneath it — the same “keep adding layers” habit you’ve been using since the first ggplot2 scatter plot.

title: 10  Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet
text:
10.4 Saving and exporting
An interactive map only stays interactive where something can run JavaScript — a rendered HTML report, a Shiny app, a browser. Paste it into a Word document or a PDF and it becomes a flat image anyway, so mapview::mapshot() lets you export either format depending on where the map is going.
Save the fully interactive version as its own HTML file — useful when you want to embed it in a Quarto HTML report with an <iframe>, or email it to someone who can open it and click around themselves:

mapshot(
  ct_case_map,
  url = here(
    "chapters",
    "03-data-visualization",
    "maps",
    "ct-case-rate-map.html"
  )
)

Save a static snapshot as PNG when the destination can’t run JavaScript at all — a slide deck, a printed briefing, a PDF report:

mapshot(
  ct_case_map,
  file = here(
    "chapters",
    "03-data-visualization",
    "maps",
    "ct-case-rate-map.png"
  )
)

Rule of thumb: if the report renders to HTML and the reader is looking at a screen, keep the map interactive. If it renders to PDF, Word, or a printed page, export a PNG instead.






Note



This section covered enough leaflet to build a colored, clickable choropleth. leaflet can also layer multiple datasets, add custom basemaps, cluster hundreds of markers, and respond to clicks with Shiny — Further Reading has a deeper dive into leaflet waiting for when you need it.

title: 11  Building This Week’s Briefing Deck
section: 11.2 Step 1 — Hartford vs. the statewide average
text:
11.2 Step 1 — Hartford vs. the statewide average
A single town’s trend only means something next to a baseline. Build Hartford’s daily new-case series, then a statewide daily average, and stack them into one tibble so both can be mapped to the same color aesthetic.

hartford_trend <-
  covid_clean |>
  filter(town == "Hartford") |>
  select(last_update_date, new_cases) |>
  mutate(series = "Hartford")

statewide_trend <-
  covid_clean |>
  group_by(last_update_date) |>
  summarise(new_cases = mean(new_cases, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(series = "Statewide Average")

combined_trend <- bind_rows(hartford_trend, statewide_trend)







Note



new_cases is the day-over-day change in total_cases, computed with lag() back in setup, grouped by town so one town’s data never bleeds into another’s. See chapter 1’s project for why this number can come out negative on a day the state revises an earlier total — real pandemic reporting data, this dataset included, is rarely clean enough to avoid that.



ggplot(
  data = combined_trend,
  mapping = aes(x = last_update_date, y = new_cases, color = series)
) +

The lesson’s choropleth mapped case_rate — cumulative cases per 100,000 people. The Commissioner’s packet already has that map from chapter 3.   mutate(positivity = number_of_positives / number_of_tests * 100) |>

title: 13  Version Control
text:
13.1 What Git Is
You have a project folder with a script and a data file in it. Right now, the only history of that project is whatever you remember. This chapter fixes that.
This is a gentle introduction — just enough to work safely day to day. Remotes and collaborating with a team on GitHub are worth exploring once this part feels comfortable, but they’re beyond what we cover here. For now: what git is, why it matters, how to install it, enough command line to drive it, the everyday workflow, and branches.
Git is a tool that saves snapshots of a folder over time, on purpose, with a note attached to each one.
If you’ve ever used “Track Changes” in Word, or kept files named report_v1.docx, report_v2.docx, report_FINAL.docx, report_FINAL_really.docx — you’ve already felt the problem git solves. Instead of guessing which version is current, git keeps every saved snapshot, labeled, in order, forever. You choose when to save a snapshot (that’s called a commit), and you write a short note explaining why.
A few terms you’ll see everywhere:

title: 13  Version Control
text:
Term
Meaning




Repository (repo)
A project folder that git is tracking


Commit
A saved snapshot of the whole folder, plus a message


Staging
Choosing which changes go into the next commit


History
The full list of commits, oldest to newest

title: 13  Version Control
text:
13.2 Why It’s Important
It’s an audit trail. Every commit records what changed, when, and why. When someone asks “where did this number come from,” you don’t just show the script — you show exactly which version of the script produced it.
It’s a safety net. Made a change that broke everything? Every previous commit is still there. You can always get back to a version that worked.
It’s how modern teams share code. Emailing zip files back and forth doesn’t scale past one person. Git — paired with a hosting service like GitHub — is how public health teams, CDC, and academic epi groups actually collaborate on code today.
It catches the honest mistakes. A filter that quietly drops a few towns, a column overwritten by accident, a formula copied one row short — these hide easily in a file that only ever gets edited in place, with nothing kept of what it looked like an hour ago. With git, “wait, when did this change, and what did it look like before” stops being a guessing game and becomes a git log and a diff.

title: 13  Version Control
text:
13.3 Installing Git






TipInstall git before continuing




Windows: download and run the installer from git-scm.com. Accept the defaults.
macOS: open Terminal and run git --version. If it isn’t already installed, macOS will prompt you to install the Xcode Command Line Tools — accept that.
Linux: use your package manager, e.g. sudo apt install git (Debian/Ubuntu) or sudo dnf install git (Fedora).



Once installed, confirm it worked:
git --version
You should see something like git version 2.43.0. Exact number doesn’t matter — any reasonably recent version is fine.
One-time setup, so your commits are labeled with your name:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

title: 13  Version Control
text:
13.4 Intro to the Command Line
Git’s full power lives on the command line. RStudio and Positron both have a Terminal tab/pane (next to the Console) — that’s a command line sitting right inside your IDE. Open it now; you’ll use it for the rest of this chapter.
A few commands you’ll lean on, regardless of operating system:



Command
What it does




pwd
Print working directory — where am I right now?


ls (dir on Windows)
List files in the current folder


cd folder-name
Change directory — move into folder-name


cd ..
Move up one level



The terminal always has a current location, same idea as here() from chapter 1 but for the shell instead of R. Before running git commands, make sure you’re inside your project folder:
cd covid-briefing
pwd

title: 13  Version Control
text:
13.5 The Happy Path Workflow
This is the loop you’ll repeat, day in and day out. Five steps.

13.5.1 1. Turn a folder into a repository — once
Inside covid-briefing/:
git init
This creates a hidden .git folder. That’s git’s database — all your history lives there. You only run git init once per project.


13.5.2 2. Check what’s changed
git status
This is your most-used git command. It tells you what’s new, what’s modified, and what git isn’t tracking yet. Run it constantly — it never changes anything, it only reports.


13.5.3 3. Stage the changes you want to save
git add scripts/01_import.R
Staging means “include this file in the next commit.” You can stage one file, several, or everything:
git add .
git add . stages every changed file in the current folder and below. Fine for now — the difference between staging some files versus all of them matters more once you’re working with others, which is a further-reading topic.


13.5.4 4. Commit — save the snapshot
git commit -m "Import raw COVID data and inspect structure"
The -m flag attaches your message right there. Write it like you’re telling a colleague what you did and why — future you is that colleague.


13.5.5 5. Review the history
git log
This lists every commit: who, when, and the message. git log --oneline gives you a compact one-line-per-commit view once your history grows.






NoteThe mental model



Three places your work can live: the working directory (files on disk, as you’re editing them), the staging area (what you’ve marked for the next commit with git add), and the repository (committed history, safe in .git). git status tells you what’s in each. git add moves changes to staging. git commit moves staging into history.




13.5.6 Putting it together
A normal working session looks like this:
git status               # see what changed
git add data/processed/  # stage the files you want to save
git status                # confirm what's staged
git commit -m "Clean town names and drop test rows"
git log --oneline         # confirm it landed
Repeat that loop every time you reach a working, meaningful checkpoint — not just at the end of the day. Small, frequent commits with clear messages are worth far more later than one giant commit called “updates.”

title: 13  Version Control
text:
13.6 Branches
So far your commits have piled up in a single line, one after another, on a branch called main. That’s the default name git gives the line of history you start with.
A branch is a second line of history that splits off from main. You commit onto the branch instead of onto main, so main sits exactly where it was — still working, still the version you’d hand to someone — while you experiment somewhere else.
Here’s the concrete case. Your covid-briefing/ project already produces a choropleth of case rate by town, and that map went out in last week’s briefing. Now you want to see whether test positivity tells a better story. That means rewriting a chunk of the plotting script, and you have no idea yet if it’ll work out. You don’t want the version that produced last week’s map to be in pieces on your disk while you find out.
So put the experiment on a branch:
git switch -c try-positivity-map
The -c means “create.” That one command makes the branch and moves you onto it. From here, every commit you make lands on try-positivity-map and main stays untouched.






Notegit checkout -b does the same thing



Older tutorials and most StackOverflow answers use git checkout -b try-positivity-map. It’s the same operation. git switch is the newer, narrower command — checkout does several unrelated jobs, which is exactly why it confused people for years. Use switch; recognize checkout -b when you see it.


To see what branches exist and which one you’re on:
git branch
The current branch is marked with a *. git status tells you too, on its first line.
Work on the branch exactly the way you already know — edit, git add, git commit. When you want to look at the old version again:
git switch main






ImportantYour files on disk actually change



This surprises everyone the first time. Switching branches rewrites the contents of your project folder to match that branch. Open the plotting script after git switch main and the positivity code is gone — it’s back on try-positivity-map, safe, but not on disk right now. Switch back and it returns.
Git isn’t losing your work. The folder is just showing you one branch at a time. Commit before you switch, and nothing goes missing.


Say the positivity map turns out better and you want it to become the real version. Go to main and merge the branch in:
git switch main
git merge try-positivity-map
main now contains the branch’s commits. The experiment graduated.
Once it’s merged, the branch has served its purpose and you can clean it up:
git branch -d try-positivity-map
The lowercase -d only deletes branches that have already been merged, so it won’t quietly throw away work you haven’t brought over yet.



Command
What it does




git switch -c name
Create a branch and move onto it


git branch
List branches, * marks the current one


git switch main
Go back to main


git merge name
Bring name’s commits into the current branch


git branch -d name
Delete a branch you’ve already merged



One thing you’ll eventually hit: if two branches changed the same lines of the same file, git can’t decide which version wins and asks you to sort it out. That’s a merge conflict. Working alone on one branch at a time, you’ll rarely see one — and resolving them is a topic for when you start sharing work with other people.






Note



This chapter stops at your local history, and local history is genuinely enough to work safely on your own — snapshots, an audit trail, and room to experiment. When you’re ready to share your work or collaborate with colleagues, pushing your repository to GitHub is the natural next step.

title: 14  Working with APIs and Functions
text:
14.1 What is an API!?
To put it simply, an API1 or application programming interface can be thought of as another tool in your tool belt to programmatically interact with and often extract data without having to manually download it. You don’t need to lift your mouse and search through a webpage and click download. This is a simple, yet powerful concept that extends to many areas of data work and beyond. There’s a lot more to APIs than what’s covered here, and it’s well worth digging further into on your own.

text:
14.2 Working with httr2
We will be working with httr2 as our package of choice for API work. Often, specific APIs will have their own packages for working with them, and it is often better to use those, but we cannot cover them all, and not every API has its own package. httr2 will always be here for you, and if you can understand httr2 then picking up other, more specific packages will become even easier.
Remember our COVID-19 pandemic dataset? Before, you would navigate to that website and download the data file, or perhaps rely on the snippet of data provided in this course. No more - you are far too busy for that kind of work. From here on out we will be using the API, and in the future when you encounter data you want to incorporate into your analyses, it is almost always better to use the API.
Install httr2 like we would any other package.

install.packages('httr2')

Next we’ll attach the httr2 and dplyr packages to our session.

library(dplyr) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages() # this silences dplyr messages when loading the package
library(httr2)


14.2.1 httr2 requests and responses
Recall our pandemic data’s landing page - notice what pops up when you click the ‘Export’ button in the top right of the webpage. The popup has ‘Download file’ defaulting to ‘Export format’ of csv. However, right next to it is ‘API endpoint’ - click that and notice the ‘Data format’ switches to ‘JSON’. Below that you may notice that there is a ‘Version’ toggle for either ‘SODA3’ or ‘SODA2’. For now, select ‘SODA2’ and copy the url provided, it should look like this: https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json now that we have our url or endpoint as they are often called let’s hop into the code.

# save our url into an object so we don't have to type it out everywhere
endpoint <- "https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json"

# We build our data request up piece by piece

my_request <- request(endpoint) # base of the request

# Get a our response from the Open Data Portal API

odp_response <-
  my_request |>
  req_perform() # perform the request, and get a response base

title: 14  Working with APIs and Functions
text:
14.3 Extracting all data
We’re going to have to do a little leg work here to get all the data, and then we’ll package it all up so you can reuse it over and over again.
First, you need to understand what the limit and offset are and how you can leverage those to get the data you expect.

limit: The total number of rows of data brought back in the request.

The default for this API and this endpoint is 1000. Some datasets might be small like 5000 rows. You can just bump this number up to 5000 and pull it all in one go.

offset: The starting point row number for the query.

The default for this API is 0, because it starts at the first row.


These two parameters can be used in conjunction to, for example, grab the first 1000 rows of a dataset, and then grab the next 1000 and so on and so forth until all data is had.

14.3.1 Modifying the limit and offset
So modifying the limit and offset is all well in good, but how do we actually go about changing those values? Remember our endpoint url? Thankfully these are parameters that can be tacked on to the end of the url.
If for whatever reason we wanted the 10th row, and only the 10th row of our dataset we can modify our url to look like this:
https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json?$limit=1&$offset=9
Notice that the parameters come at the end of the original url after a ?. You then append $limit= and & and $offset= with the desired values. Feel free to try this in your web browser - most modern browsers will display the data from the response.






Note



Note that items/data are zero-indexed, meaning the first item the data is ‘row’ 0. To grab the 10th item we skip the first 9 items.


See for yourself: click on https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json?$limit=10&$offset=0 and make note of the tenth item.

14.3.2 Using httr2
No one wants to modify urls by hand, and we’re still clicking through everything, time to use httr2 to do the heavy lifting.

# We're going to grab first 5000 rows, 1000 rows at a time.
# so we will query 1000 rows, 5 times

req <-
  request(endpoint) |>
  # don't forget the $ as part of the parameter name for this api
  # backticks are required for nonstandard r names
  req_url_query(
    `$limit` = 1000,
    `$offset` = 0
  )


resps <-
  req_perform_iterative(
    req,
    next_req = iterate_with_offset(
      param_name = "$offset",
      start = 0,
      offset = 1000
    ),
    max_reqs = 5
  )

# resps contains a list of 5 responses
# we want to take each response and do what we did above to all of them
# we will use an anonymous function otherwise known as lambda functions in
# other programming languages

data <-
  resps |>
  resps_data(
    \(resp) {
      # declare the name of each item in our resps list
      resp |> # for each response in our responses
        resp_body_json() |> # convert the json to a list
        bind_rows() # bind these into a dataframe

Wait - weren’t we promised all the data!? Fair point, how do we grab that data if we don’t know how many rows there are? At time of writing there were about 102,000 rows in this dataset, but let’s pretend we do not know that, and often that is the case.

# first request grabs the first 10k

  request(endpoint) |>

    `$offset` = 0

  req_perform_iterative(
    req,
    progress = FALSE, # the progress bar is super cool, but doesn't play nicely with the website, feel free to leave it on!

Notice we printed the row count rather than checking it against a number typed into the script. This dataset is an archive, so it’s stable, but live endpoints rarely are: rows get added, corrected, and occasionally removed. Hardcoding “there should be 102,245 rows” is the kind of check that quietly starts failing months later for a reason that has nothing to do with your code.






Warning



Start small when working with a new endpoint
You will often want all the data, but you’ll often not know how many rows there are. Use caution when grabbing everything, there may be more data than can be handled at once.

text:
14.4 Functions crash course
By now you may have noticed that you’ve written the same or similar chain of request and response a few times now. Let’s tidy this up into something you can reuse over and over - a function! The httr2 documentation has a wonderful section on wrapping apis into useful functions, and it’s well worth reading.
We will take much of the logic and code discussed in that document and apply it to our usecases.
Up to this point you’ve been using functions all over the place in R. Now you’re going to write your own using the function() function to encapsulate our logic. We will do this time and time again. We create our function by providing the inputs it expects, and then perform the actions we want it to do with those inputs. Good functions typically will do one thing or step really well, and have a descriptive name. It is usually good to create and chain a few smaller functions instead of having one massive function.
Let’s start by creating a function that reduces the amount of repetitive typing we need to do, smooths over some API rough edges and finally returns all the data.
Take one more look at our endpoint: https://data.ct.gov/resource/28fr-iqnx.json. Notice anything? If you’re always using the Open Data Portal, the domain (data.ct.gov) is always going to be the same. There is always going to be a ‘/resource/’ section and always a ‘.json’. The only real part that is going to change is the resource id (often called a four by four on this portal). That’s a good candidate for an argument to your function.

# our function will be called fetch all data
fetch_all_data <-
  function(resource, rows = 10000) {
    # Fetch all data from the provided resource id for the CT Open Data Portal
    #
    # resource: string - Required portal "four by four" in the format 'xxxx-xxxx'
    # rows: numeric - Number of rows of data to fetch one response at a time.
    #   defaults to 100000 and becomes the LIMIT and OFFSET for the request.
    # Returns: A tibble

    # handle the resource from the user

    base <- "https://data.ct.gov/resource"

    # create the first request
    req <-
      request(base) |>
      req_url_path_append(resource) |> #appened the user provided 4x4 to the base url
      req_url_query(
        `$limit` = rows, # use the default rows=10000 or what ever the user provided
        `$offset` = 0 # start with the first row
      )

    # perform the request and then with each request increment the offset by `rows`
    resps <-
      req_perform_iterative(
        req,
        progress = FALSE,
        next_req = iterate_with_offset(
          param_name = "$offset",
          start = 0,
          offset = rows # use the default rows=10000 or what ever the user provided
        )
      )

    # convert the response objects from the API to a tibble of data
    # for each response from the API grab the json body, convert to an R list
    # and then squash all that into a singular tibble
    data <-
      resps |>
      resps_data(
        \(resp) {
          resp |>
            resp_body_json() |>
            bind_rows()
        }
      )

    return(data)
  }

library(httr2)
library(lubridate)

RESOURCE <- "28fr-iqnx"

# === functions ===

  function(resource, rows = 10000) {

    #

    # rows: numeric - Number of rows of data to fetch one response at a time.
    #   defaults to 100000 and becomes the LIMIT and OFFSET for the request.
    # Returns: A tibble

    # handle the resource from the user

    base <- "https://data.ct.gov/resource"

    # create the first request
    req <-
      request(base) |>
      req_url_path_append(resource) |> #append the user provided 4x4 to the base url
      req_url_query(
        `$limit` = rows, # use the default rows=10000 or what ever the user provided
        `$offset` = 0 # start with the first row
      )

    # perform the request and then with each request increment the offset by `rows`
    resps <-
      req_perform_iterative(
        req,
        progress = FALSE,
        next_req = iterate_with_offset(
          param_name = "$offset",
          start = 0,
          offset = rows # use the default rows=10000 or what ever the user provided
        )
      )

    # convert the response objects from the API to a tibble of data
    # for each response from the API grab the json body, convert to an R list
    # and then squash all that into a singular tibble
    data <-
      resps |>
      resps_data(
        \(resp) {
          resp |>
            resp_body_json() |>
            bind_rows()
        }
      )

    return(data)
  }

# === main ===
main <- function() {
  # main entrypoint into our analysis

  # data ingestion
  data <- fetch_all_data(resource = RESOURCE)

  # key measures
  total_tests <-
    data |>
    mutate(date = ymd_hms(lastupdatedate)) |>
    filter(date == max(date)) |>
    reframe(
      total_pandemic_tests = sum(
        as.numeric(numberoftests),
        na.rm = TRUE
      )
    ) |>
    pull(total_pandemic_tests)

  cat(
    paste(
      "The total number of pandemic tests in these data were:",
      format(total_tests, big.mark = ',')
    )
  )
}

# === entrypoint ===
main()

One constant, one fetch function, one main() - a script you can hand to someone else, and the only thing they need to know to run it is that last line.

title: 16  Managing Secrets
text:
16.1 What are Secrets
Secrets are pieces of information - API keys, passwords, tokens, connection strings - that grant access to something and should never end up in your script, your git history, or your rendered output. The moment a secret is typed directly into a .R or .qmd file, it is one git push away from being public forever, even if you delete it in a later commit. History remembers.
The fix isn’t complicated: keep secrets out of code and load them in at runtime from somewhere code doesn’t normally look - an environment variable.

title: 16  Managing Secrets
text:
16.2 .Renviron
R users will often bump into .Renviron first. It’s a plain text file, usually living in your project root or your home directory, that R reads automatically on startup and turns into environment variables.

# .Renviron
CENSUS_API_KEY=abc123yourkeyhere

Restart your R session and the value is available via Sys.getenv():

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")

.Renviron works, but it’s R-specific - the skill doesn’t transfer. Learn this pattern and it’s only useful the next time you open RStudio or Positron. For that reason we’re going to spend most of this chapter on .env instead, a convention almost every language and tool understands.

title: 16  Managing Secrets
text:
16.3 .env and the dotenv package
A .env file is the same idea as .Renviron - KEY=value pairs, one per line - but it isn’t R-specific. Python, Node, Docker, and most CI systems all read .env files the same way. Learn it once here, reuse it everywhere else in your career.

# .env
CENSUS_API_KEY=abc123yourkeyhere







Important



Add .env to your .gitignore before you ever put a real value in it. An untracked file can’t leak.


R doesn’t read .env automatically the way it reads .Renviron, so we install a small package to bridge the gap.

install.packages("dotenv")

dotenv::load_dot_env() reads the file and populates the environment for the current session:

library(dotenv)
load_dot_env(".env")

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")


16.3.1 Worked example: the Census API key
The US Census Bureau’s API is a good real-world case - it’s free, it’s public-health relevant, and it requires a key. Sign up, drop the key in .env as CENSUS_API_KEY, and never type it into a script again.

library(dotenv)
library(httr2)

load_dot_env(".env")

census_key <- Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY")

request("https://api.census.gov/data/2020/dec/pl") |>
  req_url_query(
    get = "P1_001N,NAME",
    `for` = "state:09", # Connecticut
    key = census_key
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

Anyone reading this script sees that a key is required and where it comes from - but never the key itself. Share the script freely; the .env file stays on your machine.

title: 16  Managing Secrets
text:
16.4 keyring: secrets outside any file
.env still means a secret sits somewhere on disk in plain text. The keyring package goes a step further by storing secrets in your operating system’s own credential store - Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, the Secret Service on Linux. Nothing is ever written to a project file at all.

install.packages("keyring")
library(keyring)

# store it once, interactively - you'll be prompted, it won't appear
# in your script or console history
key_set("census_api_key")

# retrieve it whenever you need it
census_key <- key_get("census_api_key")

keyring is a good fit for secrets you use across many projects on your own machine - a personal API key, a database password - where per-project .env files would mean re-entering the same value over and over.

title: 16  Managing Secrets
section: 16.5 httr2::secret_encrypt(): sharing secrets safely in code
text:
16.5 httr2::secret_encrypt(): sharing secrets safely in code
.env and keyring both assume the secret lives outside what you share. Sometimes that’s not enough - a package or a shared script needs to ship with a credential built in, for a demo API or a service account that isn’t sensitive on its own but shouldn’t be plain text either. httr2 provides secret_encrypt() for exactly this case.
The idea: encrypt the secret with a key, commit the encrypted value, and keep the encryption key itself in an environment variable that never gets committed.

library(httr2)

# generate an encryption key once, store it as an env var
# (e.g. MY_PACKAGE_KEY in .Renviron or .env - never in code)
secret_make_key()


# encrypt the real secret using that key
encrypted_census_key <- secret_encrypt(
  "abc123yourkeyhere",
  "MY_PACKAGE_KEY"
)

encrypted_census_key
#> [1] "encrypted:5f8a2c..."

That encrypted:... string is safe to commit - it’s useless without the MY_PACKAGE_KEY environment variable to decrypt it. At request time, decrypt on the fly:

request("https://api.census.gov/data/2020/dec/pl") |>
  req_url_query(key = secret_decrypt(encrypted_census_key, "MY_PACKAGE_KEY"))

This is the pattern httr2 itself recommends for package authors who need to ship example code that actually runs in CI without exposing the underlying credential. For a deeper dive, see the httr2 article on wrapping APIs.

title: 16  Managing Secrets
text:
16.6 Picking an approach

One-off project, R only: .Renviron is fine.
One-off project, skill you want to transfer beyond R: .env + dotenv.
Secret reused across many projects on your machine: keyring.
Secret that needs to travel with shared code or a package: httr2::secret_encrypt().

Whichever you choose, the rule doesn’t change: secrets live in the environment, not in the script.

17.3 Custom themes and color palettes
The chapters use stock ggplot2 themes and plain hex codes so the code runs in your project with nothing extra to install. This book’s own figures are styled with a small set of CT DPH brand helpers, kept in preamble-themes.R at the root of the book’s repository.
If you work at DPH — or you just want to see how a house style gets packaged up — this section is the reference. These aren’t part of ggplot2; you’d source() the file into your own project to use them.

17.3.1 Theme functions

What it does
Use when…




theme_ct_vertical()
Removes the y-axis line, y-axis tick marks and x-axis tick marks. Sets axis titles in bold.

Theme functions stack — call them with + like any other ggplot2 layer. Later themes fill gaps left by earlier ones, so the ordering matters only when they overlap.

  labs(x = "Case status", y = "New cases", fill = "Case status") +

title: 18  Joins
text:
18.1 left_join(): keep everything on the left
The choropleth section used left_join() to attach COVID case data to town boundaries. That’s one of six join verbs dplyr gives you — each answers a different question about how two tables relate. This page walks through all six using the same shape of data: a towns table (the “left” table, like ct_towns) and a cases table (the “right” table, like town_cases).
towns has four rows, cases has three, and only two names (Hartford, New Haven) appear in both. Norwalk has no case data. Stamford has case data but isn’t in towns. That mismatch is exactly what makes joins interesting — each verb handles it differently.
towns |>
  left_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  name       county    case_rate
  <chr>      <chr>         <dbl>
1 Hartford   Hartford        412
2 New Haven  New Haven       388
3 Bridgeport Fairfield        NA
4 Norwalk    Fairfield        NA
Every row from towns survives. Where cases has no matching name (Norwalk), case_rate comes back NA. Stamford never appears — it wasn’t in the left table to begin with. This is what the choropleth uses: keep all 169 CT towns, fill in case data where it exists, show gray for the rest.

title: 18  Joins
section: 18.2 right_join(): keep everything on the right
text:
18.2 right_join(): keep everything on the right

towns |>
  right_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  name      county    case_rate
  <chr>     <chr>         <dbl>
1 Hartford  Hartford        412
2 New Haven New Haven       388
3 Stamford  <NA>            355


The mirror image. Every row from cases survives, including Stamford, which now shows NA for county. Norwalk drops out entirely since it’s not in cases. In practice, right_join(x, y) is the same as left_join(y, x) with the columns reordered — most people just pick whichever table they name first and use left_join().

title: 18  Joins
text:
18.3 inner_join(): keep only matches

towns |>
  inner_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  name      county    case_rate
  <chr>     <chr>         <dbl>
1 Hartford  Hartford        412
2 New Haven New Haven       388


Only rows present in both tables survive: Hartford and New Haven. No NAs, because everything left in the result has a match on both sides. Use this when a row without a match is meaningless for what you’re calculating — e.g., a rate that requires both a population and a case count.

title: 18  Joins
text:
18.4 full_join(): keep everything from both

towns |>
  full_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  name       county    case_rate
  <chr>      <chr>         <dbl>
1 Hartford   Hartford        412
2 New Haven  New Haven       388
3 Bridgeport Fairfield        NA
4 Norwalk    Fairfield        NA
5 Stamford   <NA>            355


Nothing is dropped. Norwalk keeps its row with case_rate as NA; Stamford keeps its row with county as NA. Use this when you want a complete picture of every name that shows up anywhere, gaps and all.

title: 18  Joins
text:
18.5 semi_join(): filter, don’t add columns

towns |>
  semi_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  name      county   
  <chr>     <chr>    
1 Hartford  Hartford 
2 New Haven New Haven


semi_join() keeps rows from towns that have a match in cases — but it never adds cases’ columns. The result has only name and county. Think of it as a filter, not a join: “give me the towns that also appear in my case data.”

title: 18  Joins
text:
18.6 anti_join(): the opposite filter

towns |>
  anti_join(cases, by = "name")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  name       county   
  <chr>      <chr>    
1 Bridgeport Fairfield
2 Norwalk    Fairfield


The inverse of semi_join(): keep rows from towns that have no match in cases. This is the fastest way to answer “which towns are missing case data?” — exactly the gray towns in the choropleth.






TipPicking the right join




Need every row from your main table, filled in where possible? → left_join()
Need only rows that exist on both sides? → inner_join()
Need every row from either side, gaps and all? → full_join()
Just need to filter one table by presence in another, without adding columns? → semi_join() / anti_join()

19.1 Installing the packages
Excel files are everywhere in public health. This chapter covers reading and writing .xlsx files using readxl and writexl.

text:
19.2 Reading .xlsx files
readxl reads Excel files the same way readr reads CSVs. Use here() to build the path so it works both interactively and during render.

library(readxl)
library(here)

xlsx_path <- here("data", "raw", "your-file.xlsx")
your_data <- read_excel(xlsx_path)

your_data

If your workbook has multiple sheets, use the sheet argument:

your_data <- read_excel(xlsx_path, sheet = "Sheet2")

# or by position
your_data <- read_excel(xlsx_path, sheet = 2)

text:
19.3 Writing .xlsx files
writexl writes a data frame to an Excel file with no Java dependency (unlike openxlsx).

library(writexl)
library(here)

output_path <- here("data", "my-output.xlsx")

write_xlsx(your_data, path = output_path)

To write multiple sheets in one workbook, pass a named list:

write_xlsx(
  list(
    cases  = cases_data,
    deaths = deaths_data
  ),
  path = output_path
)

section: 19.4 When to use CSV vs Excel
text:
19.4 When to use CSV vs Excel
Prefer CSV for anything that feeds into analysis — it is plain text, version-control friendly, and readable by every tool. Use Excel output when the end recipient is a stakeholder who will open the file directly in Excel and expects formatting.

title: 20  Reading Data: Formats and Gotchas
text:
20.1 Formats at a glance
Data shows up in a lot of shapes. A CSV emailed from a hospital, an Excel workbook from a lab, a Microsoft Access database that’s been passed around a program for a decade. R can read all of these, but a stakeholder’s very fair question is: once it’s in R, does the data need reformatting, and does that depend on the file type?
The short version: the file type changes how you read it — which package and function you reach for — but most of the cleanup headaches are the same no matter where the data came from. Dates come in as text, column names arrive messy, and blank cells mean different things to different systems. Those quirks follow the data around regardless of format.
This page is the reference for those cross-cutting quirks. For the actual how-to of reading files, you’ve already seen it:
This page is about the gotchas that come after the read.
Here are the formats an epidemiologist meets most often, the function that reads each one, and the quirks that come with the territory.
Databases deserve an honest note rather than a full tutorial. Reading directly from Microsoft Access (or SQL Server, or similar) means connecting to it with the DBI package plus a backend like odbc, and that in turn needs a database driver installed on your machine — which is frequently Windows-specific and not always something you can install yourself. The pragmatic path, and the one worth trying first, is to open the database and export the table you need to CSV, then read that CSV with the tools you already know. A fuller treatment of connecting to databases from R is a good candidate for a later chapter.

title: 20  Reading Data: Formats and Gotchas
text:
20.2 The gotchas

20.2.1 Dates read in as text
This is the one that trips up almost everyone. Unless you tell it otherwise, R will read a column of dates as plain character text. A value like 06/30/2026 is just a string of characters as far as R is concerned — you can’t do date math on it, sort it chronologically, or filter a date range until it’s been parsed into a real date.
Parsing is exactly what lubridate is for. You tell it the order the pieces appear in — month, day, year — and it handles the rest:

library(lubridate)

mdy("06/30/2026") # month-day-year
ymd("2026-06-30") # year-month-day

There’s no format string to memorize; the function name spells out the order. The Cleaning Data chapter walks through this on the real COVID dataset.






WarningExcel’s date serial-number trap



Excel doesn’t store dates as text at all — it stores them as a serial number counting days from an internal start date. Most of the time readxl converts these back to dates for you, but if a column has mixed content, or the cell was formatted oddly, dates can arrive in R as bare numbers like 44927.
If you open a “date” column and find integers around 40000–46000, that’s almost certainly an Excel serial number. You can convert it back with as.Date(44927, origin = "1899-12-30"). When you spot this, it’s worth going back to the source workbook to confirm what those numbers are supposed to mean before trusting the conversion.




20.2.2 Variable (column) names
R is picky about names, and data files rarely respect its rules. A “clean” R name — what R calls a syntactic name — must:

not start with a number (2020_cases is illegal; cases_2020 is fine),
contain no spaces (Total Cases breaks),
avoid most punctuation (%, #, /, ( and friends are out; underscores and dots are allowed),
and remember that names are case-sensitive (Town and town are two different things).

R won’t refuse to hold a messy name — it just forces you to wrap it in backticks every single time you refer to it:

# a column literally named "Total Cases" with a space
covid_data |>
  select(`Total Cases`)

Typing backticks around every reference gets old fast. The fix is janitor::clean_names(), taught in the Cleaning Data chapter. It lowercases everything, swaps spaces for underscores, and strips the problem characters in one call:

library(janitor)

covid_data <- clean_names(covid_data)
# "Total Cases" becomes total_cases, no backticks needed ever again

On length: R technically allows very long names, but keep them short and readable anyway. Some export formats and downstream tools quietly truncate long names, and a column called n_confirmed is easier to live with than number_of_confirmed_cases_reported_this_week.


20.2.3 Case sensitivity bites twice
Case sensitivity isn’t just a naming rule — it applies to the data values too. To R, "Hartford", "hartford", and "HARTFORD" are three different strings. That has two practical consequences:

Filtering silently misses rows. filter(town == "hartford") returns nothing if the data stores "Hartford".
Joins silently drop matches. If one table has "New Haven" and another has "NEW HAVEN", those rows won’t line up, and you may not notice the gap until your counts look wrong.

The defense is to normalize case before you filter or join, using stringr’s case helpers (also from the Cleaning Data chapter):

library(stringr)

str_to_lower("HARTFORD") # "hartford"  — good for matching
str_to_title("new haven") # "New Haven" — good for display

A common pattern is to lowercase both sides of a join key so the match doesn’t depend on how each source happened to capitalize things.


20.2.4 Blanks, empties, and “missing”
An empty cell is more ambiguous than it looks, and different systems disagree on what it means. When R reads a file, a “missing” value might arrive as any of:








What’s in the file
How R may see it
What it means




truly empty cell
NA
no value recorded


empty text ""
"" (empty string)
a value that happens to be blank text


the literal text NA, N/A, ., Unknown
a character string
a placeholder someone typed for missing



That last row is the trap. If a source system writes "N/A" or . (a convention SAS users will recognize) into blank cells, R reads them as ordinary text, not as missing. A count of missing values will say zero, and any numeric column with "N/A" sprinkled in will refuse to be numeric at all.
read_csv() has an na = argument for exactly this — you list the strings that should be treated as missing:

library(readr)

# treat blanks, "NA", "N/A", and a lone "." all as missing
covid_data <- read_csv(
  csv_path,
  na = c("", "NA", "N/A", ".")
)

Why fuss over blank-versus-NA? Because it changes your numbers. An empty string "" is a real (if empty) value and gets counted; an NA does not. And functions like mean() and sum() return NA the moment a single NA is present unless you tell them to skip it with na.rm = TRUE. Getting the missing values labeled correctly up front is what makes counts, denominators, and na.rm behave the way you expect downstream. The Cleaning Data chapter covers what to do with NAs once they’re correctly identified (drop_na(), replace_na()).

text:
21.1 CSV
Once you have cleaned or summarized data, you will want to write it back out. This chapter covers the most common output formats.
write_csv() from readr is the default for analysis outputs that feed into other scripts or tools.
library(readr)

title: 21  Writing Data Files
section: 21.2 Checking and cleaning up with fs
text:
21.2 Checking and cleaning up with fs
fs lets you inspect and manage files from inside R — useful for verifying that a write succeeded or cleaning up intermediate files.

library(fs)
library(here)

# list everything in a folder
dir_ls(path = here("data", "processed"))

# check whether specific files exist
files <- dir_ls(path = here("data"), glob = "*my-new-file*")
file_exists(files)

# delete files
file_delete(files)
file_exists(files)

title: 21  Writing Data Files
text:
21.3 Parquet
Parquet is a compressed columnar format that reads and writes much faster than CSV for large datasets. It is a better default than CSV once your data exceeds a few hundred thousand rows.

install.packages("arrow")


library(arrow)
library(here)

output_path <- here("data", "processed", "ct_covid_clean.parquet")

write_parquet(your_data, sink = output_path)

# reading it back
your_data <- read_parquet(output_path)

Parquet files are not human-readable in a text editor, but they are interoperable — Python, Spark, DuckDB, and most modern data tools can read the same file.
